items._ogDesc: Nvidia’s board is meeting Wednesday evening to discuss CEO Jensen Huang’s future as its leader, two sources familiar with the matter told CNN. The latest wrinkles in the chip company’s stunning corporate scandal sent shares falling in after-hours trading.
items.body:
New York — Nvidia’s board is meeting Wednesday evening to discuss CEO Jensen Huang’s future as its leader, two sources familiar with the matter told CNN. The latest wrinkles in the chip company’s stunning corporate scandal sent shares falling in after-hours trading.

The board meeting followed a New York Times report that Huang — already under scrutiny for his relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy — had an additional extramarital relationship with a company executive.

There was some expectation among Trump administration insiders that the meeting would result in Huang being ousted after 33 years leading the company, the sources told CNN. The Wall Street Journal first reported the meeting.

Nvidia shares were trading down 8.6 per cent as of 8 p.m. ET as investors digested the developments.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment about the meeting or the Times report.

On Sunday, Nvidia’s board said it would investigate whether Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort” amid reports that he had a relationship with a woman U.S. officials believe to be a Chinese spy. Huang apologized for an extramarital affair the same day, although he did not name the other party.

Huang is without a clear No. 2 if the board decides to remove him, with the founder having previously said he does not believe in succession planning.

“Our company was built so that I know how to run it,” he told Bloomberg in 2023. “So for as long as I’m running it, that’s all that matters.”

Investors are weighing the outlook for the chipmaker that’s been at the center of the AI boom if Huang is ousted from his role. The CEO has been one of AI’s most steadfast cheerleaders and funders, and investors have flocked to Nvidia shares because of his vision for the tech boom.

Nvidia shares dropped 9.5 per cent across Monday and Tuesday after Huang’s weekend admission of extramarital affair and news of the Nvidia board’s investigation.

Shares rebounded Wednesday during trading, rising 2.9 per cent, before tumbling in after-hours trading and erasing those gains.

Nvidia shares were down 27 per cent from a peak in early October as of the market close on Wednesday, before the sharp after-hours decline.

Nvidia pioneered graphics processing units, which are semiconductor chips that are critical for AI. The company’s chips are used to power AI models, from OpenAI’s ChatGPT to Anthropic’s Claude. Nvidia is also a major player in backing massive infrastructure deals for the AI buildout.

The drop in Nvidia shares weighed on the broader market: Nasdaq 100 futures fell 0.9 per cent and S&P 500 futures fell 0.5 per cent as of 7 p.m ET.

While Nvidia shares tumbled, shares of other major semiconductor chipmakers moved higher. Advanced Micro Devices shares rose 4.5 per cent as of 7 p.m. ET, while Broadcom shares rose 2.9 per cent.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

items._ogDesc: Much of the heavy machinery is at the Nemaska Lithium plant site in Quebec, is at a standstill after majority owner Rio Tinto issued dozens of layoff notices. Workers were not the only thing effected, construction on an EV battery chain that was nearly 80 per cent complete is now forced to pause.
items.body:
BECANCOUR, QUE.- Much of the heavy machinery at the Nemaska Lithium plant site in Quebec, is at a standstill after majority owner Rio Tinto issued dozens of layoff notices. Workers were not the only thing effected, construction on an EV battery chain that was nearly 80 per cent complete is now forced to pause.

This marks the latest sign for the town of Bécancour, located in a region known as “Battery Valley,” that plans for the area to become a hub of an EV manufacturing boom may not come to fruition.

“Decisions on further investment and project timing at Bécancour will depend on the outcome of the evaluation, project economics, market conditions, and customer needs,” Rio Tinto said in a statement.

The global metal and mining giant said it remains confident in the long-term outlook for lithium processing in Quebec and Canada, despite a decline in lithium prices as global demand for battery materials and electric vehicles has slowed.

The fallout could hit the town of Bécancour, which is nestled along the shores of the St. Lawrence River halfway between Montreal and Quebec City.

The Nemaska plant is vital in Quebec’s plan to set up an EV battery manufacturing chain in the province. In the same plan, the province promised to develop Bécancour into a hub.

Slow EV sales halt economic boost

As EV batteries and plants started to set up shop in the town’s industrial park in 202, Bécancour estimated it would see a boost of 1,500 direct and 5,000 indirect jobs, including in the restaurant industry and service sector.

The population grew slightly with the arrival of workers at construction sites. To accommodate them the city planned to expand schools, build housing and even purchase new ladder trucks for the local fire station.

However, when sales of EVs slowed, some projects were paused, while others were completely scrapped. In March, Nemaska announced it would scale down the pace of building its processing plant.

Though Quebec owns 46.1 per cent of Nemaska, the province’s new government said this week it would not spend a penny more on the project for the time being.

“Our sincere hope is that this is going to work, because I don’t want to be the guy to write off the $1.1 billion we invested,” said Quebec Minister of Economic Development, Innovation and Energy Stéphane Paquet.

But many in the Bécancour area say the setbacks are simply bumps in the road that leads to electrification.

“The battery file is here to stay,” said the prefect of the region Mario Lyonnais. “I am confident that the Nemaska plant will open. When it does, we will be ready and we will continue to prepare.”

Lyonnais says the battery boom was happening very quickly and that it was hard for the municipalities in the region to keep up with the pace of scaling up services.

He says the slowdown may allow the area more time to be fully ready for the grand opening of Nemaska and for a time when EV battery manufacturing delivers the region a boost.

items.title: AI stocks rebound, and Wall Street nearly returns to where it was before last week’s sell-off
items.description: A rebound for stocks in the artificial intelligence industry lifted the U.S. market on Wednesday. The S&P 500 rose 1.3 per cent.

items._ogDesc: A rebound for stocks in the artificial intelligence industry lifted the U.S. market on Wednesday. The S&P 500 rose 1.3 per cent.
items.body:
NEW YORK — A rebound for stocks in the artificial intelligence industry lifted the U.S. market on Wednesday.

The S&P 500 rose 1.3 per cent and got close to recovering all of its brutal sell-off from last week triggered by worries about a potential slowdown for AI-related businesses. The index pulled within 2.6 per cent of its all-time high set last month.

The Nasdaq composite rallied a market-leading 1.6 per cent because of the strength for tech stocks, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 254 points, or 0.5 per cent.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

Leading the way was one of the stocks that’s been at the centre of the AI industry’s manic recent swings. CoreWeave, which rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, leaped 24.7 per cent after showing investors that it lost less money during the summer than analysts expected.

It also made announcements that could allay some of the worries dogging it and the wider industry. For one, concerns are high about how CoreWeave and other companies will handle higher interest rates in the bond market, which make borrowing money more expensive.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said his company has roughly US$9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months, along with other sources of cash to help pay its bills. That had some analysts saying it’s making progress toward being able to self-fund its business.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Worries have also been rising about a potential slowdown in the overall industry given longstanding worries about whether AI will produce enough profit and productivity to make the expensive investments worth it. Such concerns accelerated following sweeping victories for Democrats in last week’s U.S. midterm elections. The worry is that Democratic control of statehouses across the country could lead to restrictions on the construction of additional AI data centres and the industry broadly.

But CoreWeave suggested strength is continuing, at least for now, and it raised its forecast for how much revenue it expects to make this year. The number was higher than analysts expected.

Of course, many challenges remain for CoreWeave and for the AI industry broadly. But CoreWeave’s report nevertheless helped stocks across the industry claw back some of their sharp recent losses.

Micron Technology, which sells memory for computers, rallied 11.9 per cent. Broadcom rose 4 per cent. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, added 1.4 per cent.

Even Nvidia climbed 2.9 per cent.

The chip company that quickly became the face of the AI boom had been falling earlier this week for reasons that have nothing to do with the rest of the industry. Its board is investigating its CEO, Jensen Huang, after he admitted to a relationship with a businesswoman who allegedly fed intelligence and advanced chips to China.

Outside of tech, Fossil Group soared 26.7 per cent after the seller of watches, handbags and other products reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It also raised its forecast for revenue this year.

Trading elsewhere on Wall Street was more mixed.

United Airlines lost 1.8 per cent as stocks broadly felt pressure from a rise in oil prices, which recovered some of their losses from earlier in the week.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude added 1.4 per cent to US$92.76. It’s near the middle of its US$72 to US$120 range since the war with Iran sent oil prices much higher early this year.

Higher oil prices tend to push yields upward in the bond market, but the U.S. bond market was closed Wednesday in observance of Veterans Day.

Yields jumped in the bond market the day before following a worse-than-expected reading on inflation in the United States. The discouraging report raised expectations for coming hikes to interest rates by the Federal Reserve.

Higher yields mean higher rates for mortgages, and companies in the real-estate industry continued to fall Wednesday. Homebuilders D.R. Horton sank 1.5 per cent and PulteGroup slipped 0.8 per cent.

  • Latest updates on investing here

All told, the S&P 500 rose 98.45 points to 7,619.38. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 254.60 to 52,486.49, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 400.31 to 25,466.19.

In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia.

South Korea’s Kospi jumped 2.6 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng was an outlier after falling one per cent.

Stocks rose 0.5 per cent in Shanghai as China’s biggest online shopping festival, Singles Day, began Wednesday. Its sales data will offer a gauge of how strong spending is in the world’s second-largest economy.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Writers Elaine Lai and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

items.title: Ford letter to PM: Chinese EV kits must not be assembled at Brampton plant
items.description: Following the sale of Stellantis’ auto assembly plant in Brampton to defence manufacturer Roshel, Ontario Premier Doug Ford is urging the federal government to ensure Chinese-made EV kits are not assembled at the plant.

items._ogDesc: Following the sale of Stellantis’ auto assembly plant in Brampton to defence manufacturer Roshel, Ontario Premier Doug Ford is urging the federal government to ensure Chinese-made EV kits are not assembled at the plant.
items.body:
Following the sale of Stellantis’ auto assembly plant in Brampton to defence manufacturer Roshel, Ontario Premier Doug Ford is urging the federal government to ensure Chinese-made EV kits are not assembled at the plant.

In a letter obtained by CTV News dated Nov. 10, the day after the sale was announced, the premier wrote directly to the prime minister: “We cannot undermine the future of Canada and Ontario’s automotive sector by allowing the introduction of Chinese-made knock-down kits at the Stellantis Brampton facility, to which Ontario remains strongly opposed.”

“Based on our recent discussion, I welcome the federal government’s alignment with Ontario’s position.”

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

A Chinese EV kit is essentially an electric vehicle manufactured largely in China, then shipped to another country — such as Canada — in pieces to be assembled into a finished car.

On Tuesday, CTV News reported, based on sources, that Carney’s government has been actively and intensively involved in talks with Stellantis and Roshel that ended in the agreement to sell the Brampton plant.

The sources said the federal government did not stand in the way of the deal in those private discussions.

Multiple sources with knowledge of negotiations for the Brampton plant sale told CTV News Stellantis plans to re-lease 25 per cent of the plant from Roshel, to assemble “affordable” EVs for Canadian customers. The company would retain a portion of the workforce to do so.

Industry sources say they are concerned that means the assembling of Chinese EV kits, or even fully manufacturing the cars. The federal government has publicly opposed the former but not the latter.

The premier’s letter to the prime minister goes on to urge him to remain opposed to the kits.

“We must remain aligned in our efforts to protect and expand Ontario and Canada’s automotive footprint. Fortifying Ontario and Canada’s industrial base, including a strong and growing automotive sector, is foundational to creating and realizing generational economic opportunities.”

In addition to the prime minister, the letter was copied to Industry Minister Melanie Joly, Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli, Unifor National President Lana Payne, and Auto Parts Manufacturer Associate President Flavio Volpe.

In a statement sent to CTV News Wednesday, the prime minister’s spokesperson Sofia Ouslis said the federal government is aligned with Ontario in its commitment to protect workers and safeguard manufacturing in Brampton.

“We are not considering any proposal to replace full vehicle manufacturing and assembly with Chinese-made kit cars,” said Ouslis. “This has been reinforced repeatedly by Minister Joly, who has emphasised that any Chinese EV investment must use Canadian parts, Canadian labour, and a Canadian supply chain.”

Thousands of jobs at stake: premier

In his letter, Ford said replacing made-in-Canada vehicles with made-in-China kit production would lead to thousands of job losses. In Brampton alone, the premier said it would cause a direct employment loss of more than 7,500 jobs that would be replaced only by a few hundred assembly positions.

Joly has said, on multiple occasions, that she opposes the knock-down kits. In April, she told reporters in Vancouver, “We can’t bring cars in a kit to Canada. Why? Because one of the big parts of our auto industry is actually linked to the fact that we have a big auto parts sector – 200,000 workers.”

The federal government, however, is open to Chinese EVs being manufactured in Canada. In June, after meeting with four Chinese car manufacturers, Joly told reporters that all the companies she met with are “willing to explore creating joint ventures in Canada in order to produce in Canada.” The minister stipulated any arrangement would have to meet specific conditions, including a localized supply chain and Canadian control of the joint venture.

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu visited one of those Chinese automakers, Chery, and posted online that he had done so “to discuss their upcoming models and hear about their plans to introduce affordable EVs to Canadians.”

His comments were criticized by Unifor National President Lana Payne.

“Thousands of autoworkers are fighting to save their jobs, including in Minister Sidhu’s own riding of Brampton,” she wrote. “Anyone who understands the auto industry knows the problem China poses to 100000s of jobs here in Canada and across [North America] and to the entire manufacturing industry.”

Unifor is opposed to the sale of the Stellantis Brampton plant. Payne accused Stellantis of betraying its employees, “with an underhanded deal to sell the plant and walk away from its commitments to our members.”

A meeting between the union, Joly and Stellantis is scheduled for Thursday in Toronto.

In a statement to CTV News, Volpe wrote “the Premier has always understood that the industrial strength of the Ontario auto sector comes from Canadian companies that make up the supply chain. He knows that the Chinese kit proposals are a direct threat to the viability of hundreds of Canadian companies and their 100,000 workers. We appreciate that.”

items.title: Housing protests fill Barcelona and Madrid as Spain’s workers strike ahead of election
items.description: Millions of Spanish workers shut down businesses and public transportation on Wednesday in a nationwide protest over soaring rents and real estate prices.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Protestors march during a nationwide general strike in Barcelona, Spain, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Joan Mateu Parra)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Joan Mateu Parra</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Millions of Spanish workers shut down businesses and public transportation on Wednesday in a nationwide protest over soaring rents and real estate prices.
items.body:
BARCELONA, Spain — Millions of Spanish workers shut down businesses and public transportation across the eurozone’s fourth largest economy on Wednesday before thousands took to the streets of major cities in a nationwide protest over soaring rents and real estate prices.

Housing activists hope the massive show of force will lead to more regulations to protect tenants and crack down on real estate speculation, while Spain’s left-wing government is seeking to mobilize voters ahead of a national election later this month with polls against it.

The walkout -- under the slogan “Salaries. Housing. Prices.” -- was the first general strike in Spain in 14 years, and the first whose principal push was born from unrest over housing.

The strike culminated in workers and average citizens gathering in downtown Barcelona and Madrid, along with protests in other cities. Housing activists said 400,000 marchers filled Barcelona, while the city government said 55,000 turned out to walk behind a huge banner that said “Live. Not Just Survive.”

Spanish government officials estimated 120,000 people turned out in Madrid despite pouring rain.

After the peaceful march in Barcelona, some apparently younger protesters started to smash storefronts of brand-name stores on Paseo de Gracia, a main shopping boulevard. They set off small bonfires in front of stores, burned dumpsters and launched fireworks at police who arrived in riot gear and armored vans.

During the day, Barcelona’s metro and public buses stopped running outside rush hour. Street traffic was light. Many smaller establishments like coffee shops, however, did open.

Carlos Ferrer, a 45-year-old customer service worker who was trying to get back home to Alicante by train from Barcelona, said that sometimes only “radical measures, such as a general strike” can force a change of course.

“Authorities need to feel pressure from the citizens so they can do something,” he said.

Protesters march in Madrid, defying rain and pepper spray

As the evening fell in Spain’s capital, the wide Paseo del Prado boulevard became a sea of umbrellas as a huge crowd turned out during steady rain.

Almudena López, 74, and her husband attended Wednesday’s protest in Madrid thinking of their children.

“My son is 43 years old and still doesn’t own a home as he cannot afford one,” López said. She said her son, who works in IT, has to rent a small room in a shared apartment.

“When I was young, if you had a university degree, you could get a job by saving a bit — which always required some sacrifice — but you could manage. It’s nothing like it is today.”

While the strike was organized by Spain’s two traditional major unions, it featured the leadership of a grassroots housing activist group, mostly made up of younger people who have felt the housing pinch personally.

“This strike is against rent seekers, against real estate speculators, against the large companies that get rich by selling properties and, of course, against all the levels of government,” housing activist Valeria Racu told reporters in Madrid. “We are here to show that we have the capacity to mark our own agenda and we are going to keep doing so no matter who governs.”

Unions call strike a success, business owners call it a failure

Unions also hailed the strike as a success, while Spain’s business owners’ groups argued that it had fallen flat.

“The strike has exceeded the labor unions’ expectations,” said Unai Sordo, secretary-general of CCOO, one of the two unions calling the strike for a nation of 22 million registered workers.

CCOO and UGT, the other major union organizing the strike, reported significant work stoppages in strategic sectors. They said that the stoppages amounted to 90 per cent in the automotive and port sectors, 85 per cent in the meat industry, 82 per cent in waste collection and 75 per cent in the energy sector. Many schools and universities closed.

The leading business owners group, CEOE, however, called the strike a “failure,” saying that overall participation only reached 5 per cent.

Where unions and the CEOE agreed was that worker participation was higher in heavy industry and transportation, while it lagged in other sectors of the economy like retail and restaurants.

About 5 per cent of flights for Wednesday were canceled at airports across Spain, according to the country’s airport operator, AENA.

Minor incidents were reported in the first hours of the strike. Scuffles with police were reported by unions near the main wholesale market on Madrid’s outskirts. Police also used pepper spray against protesters in some places.

Police had already made 39 arrests across Spain for incidents related to the strike.

Workers and activists want more government action on housing

The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the last decade, eating into household budgets and upsetting voters.

The anger reached a boiling point following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last month. The subsequent death of Maricarmen, as the woman became known, solidified her as a symbol of Spaniards who can’t dream of owning a home.

Housing activists leveraged the uproar over Maricarmen’s eviction to call for the general strike, and soon won the union backing.

The housing activists are seeking the automatic renewals of leases as a way to protect renters and other measures. Unions demand more public housing and a new minimum wage agreement.

Spain’s left hopes to put focus back on housing

On the back of recent protests over Maricarmen’s plight, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called an early election, hoping to earn four more years in power for his left-wing coalition. The vote is set for Nov. 29.

Then, in late October came a high-speed train collision -- Spain’s second deadly rail disaster of the year -- that killed 69 people. The aftermath of the tragedy has created a drag on Sanchez’s campaign.

The strike now offers an opportunity for Sanchez’s Socialists and other parties on the left seeking to stay in power, analyst Oriol Bartomeus said.

“The Socialists need for the strike to be a success and for there not to be any violence so that the election campaign can swing back to being about housing,” Bartomeus, a professor of political science at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, told The Associated Press.

Sánchez kept a low profile on Wednesday. Earlier this week he posted a video on X lauding past social policy achievements like the 40-hour work week and national health insurance, which were the fruit of the workers’ movement.

“It wasn’t easy, but they changed Spain,” Sanchez said, warning that right-wing parties would underfund social services if they took over.

The conservative Popular Party and the far-right Vox argued that the unions were trying to help Sánchez.

“This is a gift by the unions to their political parties during the buildup to a campaign where it is clear the left needs all the help it can get,” said Popular Party spokesman Miguel Tellado.

Joseph Wilson and Teresa Medrano, The Associated Press

Associated Press journalists Hernán Muñoz in Barcelona, Spain, and Iain Sullivan in Madrid contributed to this report.

items.body:
OTTAWA — A psychologist is calling on the federal government to ban all advertising promoting sports betting while it considers a new national regulatory framework.

Bill S-211, which passed second reading in the House of Commons in April, would impose federal oversight to regulate sports betting ads.

Dr. Steven Joordens, a spokesperson for the Canadian Psychological Association, says the two-year time frame in the bill means the federal government must take action now to ban the ads.

Sen. Marty Deacon, who introduced the bill, says the ads can easily move from province to province, making them a federal concern.

Paul Burns of the Canadian Gaming Association says provinces have the best tools to deal with the issue.

If the bill passes its final reading in the House, it will move back to the Senate for a vote.

Alyssa Wheeler, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney takes off Wednesday for summits in Asia and Ireland where he’ll look to advance trade and security ties.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney takes off Wednesday for summits in Asia and Ireland where he’ll look to advance trade and security ties.

His travels will take him to four countries and put him on the ground as high-stakes diplomacy takes place between the United States, China and Russia.

Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, said the trip is Canada’s chance to build on new agreements and partnerships it has signed with countries around the world.

“We’re now entering a much more consequential phase of actually implementing and delivering on all of these agreements, and sustaining the momentum,” she said.

“When Prime Minister Carney speaks about diversifying our relationships, it’s not just about Europe.”

The prime minister is set to depart for Dublin shortly after the Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa.

Ireland

Carney will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin, set for Nov. 12. For the second time, Canada will be the only non-European country represented at the table. Carney joined the group’s last meeting in Armenia in May.

The EPC summits have taken place roughly every six months since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The informal meetings are aimed at discussing strategic co-operation in politics, security and infrastructure.

Carney and European Union leaders have floated Canada becoming an “associate member” of the EU since the last summit -- a title they have yet to define.

The Philippines

After Dublin, Carney will cross both the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans to visit Manila, where the Philippines is hosting Canada as a guest at the Nov. 15--18 summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

ASEAN is a bloc of 11 countries that focuses on trade, regional peace and international norms. Canada is set to finalize negotiations on two trade deals while Carney is in Manila, one with the ASEAN bloc and another bilateral deal with the Philippines. He could even sign one of them while he’s there.

The prime minister has a meeting scheduled for Saturday with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and will address ASEAN leaders on Sunday.

Queen’s University professor Stephanie Martel, who studies Southeast Asia and the Asia-Pacific, said the visit will help shape the Indo-Pacific strategy the Trudeau government released four years ago. That strategy focused on making Ottawa a relevant partner in the region after years of sporadic engagement.

“It’s becoming kind of a cliche to refer to Canada as this fairweather friend,” she said.

Martel said Carney has focused on trade and maritime defence but less on local concerns about climate change resilience and gender-inclusive militaries.

“There’s a lot of action in terms of specific trade deals and specific sectors. But the overall engagement and the ability of Canada to be seen as this serious, comprehensive contributor to the region is still up for debate,” she said.

In the Philippines, Carney will be joined by Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu and Gender Minister Rechie Valdez, who is of Filipino origin.

Cambodia

Carney will then visit the Francophonie summit in Cambodia set for Nov. 14 to 16. He’s expected to meet with leaders from Africa and other continents while in the capital Phnom Penh.

Canada is hosting the next Francophonie summit in 2028 in the Ottawa area. Carney is expected to use the gathering to advance Canada’s strategic autonomy and protect the role of French in the growing digital economy.

Francophonie members will elect their next leader in Cambodia and Ottawa says it is staying neutral to avoid affecting the next summit.

On Sunday, the prime minister is set to address CEOs at the FrancoTech innovation event at the summit. On Monday, he is set to give plenary remarks.

Dominique Caouette, Indo-Pacific studies chair at the University of Montreal’s political science department, said the Francophonie summit is an opportunity for Canada and Quebec to advance economic interests.

“The Francophonie could also serve as a platform for Mr. Carney toward the middle powers. There are several that are part of the Francophonie. It’s another space where Canada could play an influential role,” Caouette said in a French-language interview.

The summit will feature both Carney and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who was elected on a sovereigntist mandate aimed at pushing back on Ottawa. Caouette said he doesn’t expect the two to clash.

“It’s not in the Canadian or Quebec tradition to air one’s dirty laundry in public,” he said.

Carney will be joined in Cambodia by Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and her parliamentary secretary Mona Fortier. Before his arrival, Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour will lead Canada’s delegation at the summit.

China

Carney’s last stop will be China’s tech hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, set for Nov. 18 to 19. Leaders from across the Pacific Rim will gather in the city bordering Hong Kong to take stock of an increasingly disordered trading system.

Nadjibulla said the summit allows for bilateral and “minilateral” discussions that bring leaders together in small groups to advance common goals. She said the APEC meetings themselves have taken on less importance, thanks to the diverging interests of Russia, the U.S. and China.

U.S. President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the summit.

The meeting has European leaders worried about a possible impact on Moscow’s war against Ukraine. Analysts are also watching for any updates on Trump’s war on Iran.

Carney’s visit will come just days after China extended a deal to provide market access to Canadian imports such as canola meal and lobster, in exchange for Canadian market access for Chinese steel and aluminum.

Xi and Carney are set to meet Tuesday and he will address business leaders the next day.

Nadjibulla said she’ll be watching for any economic announcements, such as a move to allow more Chinese vehicles into Canada or new Chinese investments in energy and technology.

“The warming, the recalibration of the relationship has been moving at a rapid pace,” Nadjibulla said, adding that any moves could affect trade talks with the U.S.

In China, Carney will be joined by his parliamentary secretary Kody Blois and Anand.

Carney is set to return to Ottawa on Nov. 19.

The federal Conservatives have criticized Carney’s overseas deals, arguing that the signed agreements have not yielded significant gains and are distracting the government’s attention from the affordability crisis.

The Liberals argue facetime between leaders is critical to diversifying trade and building more resilient supply chains and security partnerships.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

items.body:
CoreWeave’s stronger third-quarter results and increased annual guidance have brought renewed attention to the AI cloud sector following a technology sell-off.

BNN Bloomberg spoke with Lorne Steinberg, co-president of Lorne Steinberg Wealth Management, about the implications for technology shares and opportunities tied to Canada’s major project buildout.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

Key Takeaways

  • Strong demand supports AI cloud growth, but financing, timely data centre construction and public policy remain key risks, Steinberg says.
  • Software valuations offer opportunities where concerns about AI disruption have outpaced evidence of business deterioration, he argues.
  • Share buybacks, asset sales and reinvestment can help software companies unlock value, while heavy AI spending can constrain near-term free cash flow.
  • Canadian equipment suppliers could benefit from infrastructure and data centre construction, with Steinberg highlighting Finning and Toromont.
  • Critical minerals, transportation and data centre projects could support engineering demand, underpinning Steinberg’s interest in WSP Global.

Read the full transcript below:

ROGER: CoreWeave showed a strong third quarter, lifting its guidance for the year. The neocloud provider has been facing pressure in recent months as investors continue to weigh a volatile tech trade. Let’s get more from Lorne Steinberg, co-president of Lorne Steinberg Wealth Management. Lorne, thanks as always for joining us.

LORNE: Thank you, Roger.

ROGER: OK, it’s been a rough little while, but a good day today for CoreWeave. What do you see they did right, and what’s driving this?

LORNE: Well, I think the No. 1 thing is the stock’s been under tremendous pressure, in large part due to the amount of money they’ve had to borrow, and the bond prices for CoreWeave have been decimated, which would have made it very difficult to raise more cash. So today’s print, I think, gives investors, first of all, a lot of comfort that CoreWeave’s revenues are on track. They’ve raised their guidance that they’re going to deliver over $13 billion of revenues this year. Their margins have improved, but I think, really significantly, they’ve indicated, Roger, that they’re only going to have to raise about $5 billion through 2027 to meet their buildout capacity that they have promised to their customers, and they should be easily able to do that at bond prices that would probably be in the seven to eight per cent range. So it’s a huge sigh of relief to investors and takes the pressure off in the near term.

ROGER: So, so what does this mean then for other, other neoclouds like Nebulas — Nebius, excuse me — and IREN?

LORNE: So, I think a lot of it has to do with the guidance provided that they are massively oversubscribed on the amount of capacity they can build out, so that, to me, makes the whole sector look very stable and strong growth for the next couple of years. I think the biggest issue going forward past, you know, ’27 or ’28 is the — of course, the midterm elections in the States, you know, indicate that we may get fewer data centres built out than are — were originally, you know, on the slate, and that could have a negative impact. The biggest tough thing for CoreWeave, but they’ve shown zero problem with this, is they have to deliver these data centres on time, or else they would be subject to penalties and possibly cancellation. But thus far, there have been — there’s been zero indication of that. So I think the industry is stable for next couple of years. But really, public policy may have some impact on the industry as a whole. But pretty positive for everybody.

ROGER: So it’s going to — it sounds like it’s going to take some work. There must — there’s opportunities, though, in these moments, isn’t there?

LORNE: Absolutely. The stock is still way down from where it was, but this gives investors a lot of comfort that the company is here to stay for the next few years. That’s for sure.

ROGER: All right. Some names that pop up for you within tech: Constellation, Open Text, Adobe, Alphabet. What are you seeing there? What do you see for opportunities there?

LORNE: So first of all, let me deal with a couple of Canadian stocks first. So Constellation Software has been a spectacular growth story, growth by acquisition, delivering, you know, 15 per cent annualized revenue growth, which we see continuing going forward. The stock was under pressure and way down from where it was. Of course, because people feared AI would cut into the need for software. But they really deal with small and medium-sized businesses to a great extent. Those companies just don’t have the capacity to do it themselves. So for us, this is — remains a great opportunity to get into one of Canada’s few real growth stories, and a company with a — you know, in a pretty unique position.

The second company is Open Text. Open Text has been a zero grower for the past few years. They switched CEOs. We like what’s going on there, but Open Text, Roger, is actually the cheapest company in our portfolio, trading at about six times earnings, delivering significant free cash flow, and the new management team has been very clear that they are there to create value finally for shareholders, and that’s starting to take the form of share — significant share buybacks, as well as investing in growth, but also divesting themselves of assets which were basically going nowhere.

On the U.S. side, let me be clear: one of the cheapest stocks we own is Adobe. Adobe, also another software company under pressure because of fears of AI, but there has been absolutely zero indication that anything is being cut out of their business. Every quarter is another 10 per cent-plus revenue and earnings grower, and at 10 times free cash flow, this company is actually buying back significant stock, and, you know, we see the stock worth double the current share price.

And, and finally, when we look at Alphabet, you know, just among the best in the world at what they do, the best in many areas. Alphabet’s been under pressure because, of course, the AI spend, the capex they’re putting out, is eating up all of their free cash flow and then some for the next couple of years. That being said, Alphabet has over five — a backlog of over $500 billion. So a lot of this capex will be producing short-term return on investment very quickly. The company’s trading at the cheapest valuation it has in many years, 15 times earnings, and revenues are growing at an astounding 25 per cent, which we expect to continue per year for the next couple of years. So this is just an incredible opportune entry opportunity to get into a company of this quality.

ROGER: OK, the other big AI, at least in Canada, the other big story — AI is everywhere, of course — but the big Canadian major project buildout. You’re seeing opportunities there. Finning showing up for you. Toromont, WSP. Some quick reasons on those ones why they’ve got your attention.

LORNE: Sure. So Toromont, Toromont and Finning are the largest Caterpillar dealers. Finning’s the largest. Toromont second. And of course, to build out all of these projects, you’re going to need a lot of equipment, and you have nowhere else to go in Canada but Finning and Toromont. So these companies already have a record backlog, and these projects haven’t even started yet. They’ll both benefit from data centre buildout, infrastructure, etc.

Interestingly, Toromont also has a division that caters specifically to data centres because they sell power supplies and in — and enclosures for data centres. Canada should be somewhat of a beneficiary if there’s some pushback in the U.S. of — in communities that don’t want to build data centres, and we’re already seeing data centre approvals here in Canada, you know, from the likes of Meta, et cetera. So both these companies are primed to deliver double-digit earnings growth for years to come. They also both happen to be dividend aristocrats, with Finning having raised its dividend every year for 25 straight years, Toromont every year for 37 straight years. So these are just two incredibly fine companies.

WSP Global, of course, is the large engineering company, and they are poised to get contracts across the board. Critical minerals as they build out the Ring of Fire, transportation, data centres. The stock has been under pressure with most engineering companies because of fears that AI would require, you know, smaller contracts from large companies. There again is zero evidence of this, and we’re looking at WSP Global to be also a double-digit grower. So here are three Canadian companies that will absolutely benefit from the buildout in Canada.

ROGER: All right, we have to wrap it up there, Lorne. But thanks as always for joining us.

LORNE: Roger, thank you so much for having me.

ROGER: Lorne Steinberg, co-president of Lorne Steinberg Wealth Management.

items._ogDesc: Canadian housing affordability improved for a record 11 quarters, but homes remain unaffordable and rising mortgage rates threaten further gains, warns NBF.
items.body:
Canadian real estate affordability just saw its longest improvement streak in history. National Bank‘s Q3 housing affordability index shows a record 11 quarters of improvements. Tragically, a long streak of minor improvements means it’s still one of the worst markets ever. The bank warns that higher mortgage rates are also likely to bring those improvements to an end.

Canadian Housing Affordability Improves For Longest Streak Ever

Monthly mortgage payment on median home price, all types of dwellings (25-year amortization, 5-year term)

Source: National Bank Financial.

Canadian housing affordability just printed its longest improvement streak ever. Mortgage payments on a typical home as a share of median household income fell 0.7 percentage points to 50.9% in Q3 2026. That means a household would spend 50.9 cents of every pre-tax dollar they make to pay a mortgage at today’s prices. While high, that’s the lowest it’s been in a while.

“Housing affordability improved for an eleventh consecutive quarter in Q3 2026, extending the longest period of gains on record,” explains National Bank economist Kyle Dahms.

The improvement was driven by lower home prices and higher incomes. A 1.0% drop in seasonally adjusted home prices in Q3 trimmed 0.5 points from the index. At the same time, the bank estimates that household income rose 0.7% in the quarter, trimming 0.4 points from the index. Together, those gains more than covered the 0.2-point erosion from rising mortgage rates in the quarter.

Affordability improved due to falling prices and higher incomes, not cheaper financing? Fascinating, but let’s put a pin in that for a moment.

Canada’s Record Affordability Gains Still Leave Housing Unaffordable

Despite the streak, actually buying a home is pretty much impossible for most of Canada. After peaking at roughly 66% of income in 2023, the index has made a sharp improvement. “The cumulative improvement since Q4 2023 now approaches 15 percentage points, although the Composite 10 remains 9.7 points above its historical average and 8.5 points higher than its pre-pandemic level,” explains Dahms.

Keep in mind that longer elevation above the average since 2000 helps to drag that number higher. Ten years ago, the average since 2000 was 31.1% of income, according to the bank’s report from then. It’s since climbed to 41.2%, meaning the baseline is worse and normalizing the lack of affordability.

That said, the bank warns this may be as good as it gets in the near term.

Soaring Mortgage Rates Threaten To Derail Improvements

Rising mortgage rates threaten to offset affordability gains. The bank’s 5-year fixed benchmark mortgage rate added 38 basis points (bps) in October, up 45 bps from its Q3 average. It was the largest monthly jump in four years, pushing the rate to its highest level since July 2024.

“All in all, housing affordability is facing in Q4 its most significant interest-rate challenge since 2022,” warns Dahms.

If home prices are flat in October, mortgage rates would add 2.4 points to the payment burden. That would be partially offset by a 0.2-point improvement from rising incomes, but still leave the index at 53.1%. What happens is anyone’s guess for the rest of the year, but the Bank of Canada (BoC) sees this continuing. The central bank warns inflation won’t return to the target rate until 2028. That’s a long return trip with higher borrowing costs along the way.

While the bank’s view is that higher rates will erode affordability, they don’t touch the outlook beyond Q4. In this very Q3 report, affordability improved alongside higher rates. Rising mortgage rates diminish credit capacity, reducing household leverage and thus liquidity. Weaker liquidity pushes prices lower, which can potentially offset the pain over time.

BoC research previously revealed that home prices absorbed savings from lower interest rates. Instead of saving on interest, prices rose to absorb the extra debt service capacity. The US Federal Reserve made a similar argument, while the BIS attributes the post-pandemic global home price surge to rates being too low for too long.

items.title: Toronto condo market recovery could still be 'two to three years' away
items.description: The sector’s years-long downturn doesn’t seem set to end in 2027
items.content: <p>The sector’s years-long downturn doesn’t seem set to end in 2027</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639300218631918153.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The sector’s years-long downturn doesn’t seem set to end in 2027
items.body:
Mortgage and housing market watchers have been waiting for years for Toronto’s beleaguered condo sector to finally gather pace – but a 2027 recovery doesn’t look to be in the cards as buyers continue to snub the space.

October saw yet another decline in condo sales and prices, and while many mortgage brokers working in the city see some opportunities for buyers among other property types, the familiar problems plaguing the condo market seem likely to persist.

Mike Kazarian (pictured top), a Toronto-based mortgage broker with Lenders’ Choice Mortgages, told Canadian Mortgage Professional he’s still been hearing of potential condo buyers facing financing challenges – and he doesn’t expect the market to see any improvement when 2027 comes around.

“I think the outlook for condos is still bad,” he said. “It’s going to be two or three years because the population growth has basically plummeted. If that continues, there’s a lot of inventory right now and a lot of the preconstruction builders are doing fire sales.”

A new federal government initiative to accelerate permanent residency for workers already living in Canada has changed the immigration picture slightly over the past week, although RBC Economics doesn’t see the change having a significant impact on housing – for now.

“Given the abundance of inventory in the housing market, a modest acceleration in population growth doesn’t introduce substantial risk to affordability near-term,” RBC economist Rachel Battaglia said in a report this week. “That said, this could quickly change as existing pent-up demand is unlocked.”

While end users and first-time buyers are still avoiding the condo sector, recent months have seen some interest emerge among bigger investors including Jesta Group, a global real estate firm that reportedly earmarked $500 million worth of Toronto condos for investment earlier this year.

Kazarian said he sees that trend continuing. “I think you’re going to see a lot of REITS [real estate investment trusts] and big companies come in and buy these condos for purpose-built rentals,” he said.

“And look, we need rentals in the city. We need to make it more affordable, but that’s not going to help out the mortgage business and people looking to buy.”

Lower prices could spark a better homebuying outlook elsewhere

One possible bright spot for the condo sector: the federal government’s recent announcement that it intends to amend the ban on non-resident foreign buyers, extending that restriction into 2029 but loosening it to exclude the purchase of newbuild homes.

Some analysts say that decision could open the door to foreign investment in the preconstruction sector, potentially putting a floor under the market’s years-long correction.

Still, it remains to be seen whether that drums up enough interest to get the market moving again – especially for microunits, the now-notorious sub-500-square-foot condos built for renting but seeing little to no interest among potential buyers who want to live in the property they purchase.

Prices have been sliding across the board in Toronto, and outside the condo sector Kazarian said he sees reason to believe homebuyers will continue to snag deals and find the right purchasing opportunity in 2027.

“I think a lot of people are going to be cautious [next year], but on the flipside of that housing prices re coming down. We’ve seen, across the GTA [Greater Toronto Area], an approximately 21% decrease in housing prices [since their 2022 peak]. So is now a good time to buy? It might be.”

Trade, inflation concerns linger as 2027 nears

Other clouds are continuing to hover over the housing outlook, though – including trade tensions with the US and the continuing US-Iran war, both of which have sparked economic fears.

The Iran war has pushed up fuel prices and raised fears of Bank of Canada rate increases caused by inflation pressure, while the ongoing trade turmoil has spiked concerns about job losses and layoffs in tariff-impacted areas.

The issue of job security is one that frequently rears its head with customers, according to Kazarian. “I’ve seen many clients where they’ll take the position that they want to make sure they can quality for the mortgage based on one income versus both because they’re just being cautious in the event that one of them loses their job,” he said.

“So I think the market will pick up, but people are going to be cautious and they’re going to be selective. I don’t think we’re going to see any kind of multiple offer situations, but I think it might be a good time to buy.”

items.title: AI to create more jobs than it eliminates by 2030: Gartner
items.description: New forecast shows impact of AI on the job market
items.content: <p>New forecast shows impact of AI on the job market</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/035/0365_639299607476918333.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: New forecast shows impact of AI on the job market
items.body:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is set to create more jobs than it eliminates by the end of the decade, according to new forecasts from Gartner.

The business and technology insights company projects that AI will generate 10.6 million new jobs and remove 8.9 million by 2030, a net increase of 1.7 million positions.

Gartner also broke down the expected impact of AI on jobs across three types of industries.

In asset-intensive industries, Gartner expects AI to create 6.4 million jobs and eliminate six million by 2030. AI-driven job losses are projected to affect 0.4% of the sector's workforce.

These industries, which deal in physical products or deliver services within capital-intensive physical infrastructure, account for the largest share of jobs globally.

The technology sector is heavily affected by AI, with nearly 70% of its workforce highly exposed. Even so, Gartner expects the sector to create 1.9 million jobs and lose 0.4 million by 2030. AI job losses are projected to represent 1.8% of the global technology workforce over the period.

The public sector is the only one of the three where Gartner forecasts more jobs lost than gained: 0.9 million losses against 0.4 million gains by 2030.

AI-driven job losses are projected to total 0.4% of the global public sector workforce. Gartner added that AI investment in the sector is unlikely to be enough to offset severe future skills shortages driven by other factors.

Gartner's findings come amid worker fears that AI will wipe out jobs. Last year, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that AI could eliminate half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and push US unemployment to between 10 and 20% in the next one to five years.

But Helen Poitevin, Distinguished VP Analyst at Gartner, said the organisations furthest along with AI are using it to rethink how they operate, not simply to cut staff.

"Organisations most advanced in AI execution view AI not as a replacement for labour, but as a catalyst to reinvent operations and rebalance workforce and technology capabilities to compete in changing markets. They ensure AI's economic value goes beyond replacing labour," Poitevin said at the Gartner IT Symposium/Xpo in Barcelona.

Hiring put on hold

Despite the positive overall outlook, Gartner's forecast points to a less visible effect of AI on the labour market: roles that are never created.

According to Gartner, one of the most significant impacts on the job market in 2026 was executives' decisions to defer the creation and hiring of 1.3 million positions. Gartner's 2026 figures also show 2.2 million jobs lost and 1.6 million gained.

By 2030, Gartner expects five million people to have experienced delayed hiring as business and IT executives postpone the creation of new positions.

"Deferred jobs are not the same as lost jobs. They simply aren't created," said John Lovelock, Distinguished VP Analyst, Chief of Research at Gartner.

Job losses limited, transformation widespread

Gartner projects that between 0.4 and 1.8% of workers will experience job loss directly attributable to AI by 2030.

Far more workers will see their roles change. Gartner estimates that just over 20% of workers, or 435.5 million employees, will have to adapt to the new shape of work through 2030. That includes changes to what they do, how they do it and where their responsibilities begin and end.

Poitevin warned employers against assuming AI will affect every part of their business in the same way.

"AI job impacts are unevenly distributed across geographies, job functions and industries. The worst mistake that a business and IT executive can make is to apply lessons from one industry or role to another which can lead to poor errors in judgement and missed targets," she said.

"Each industry faces unique challenges and risks that executive leaders must understand and address."

items.title: Insider: Developers Still Need Someone To Write The Equity Cheque
items.description:
A better loan offer won't get a stalled project built if nobody is willing to put up the equity.

That problem runs through PwC and the Urban Land Institute's Emerging Trends in Real Estate 2027. Among Canadian survey respondents, 63% expect equity for development and redevelopment to be undersupplied in 2027. For debt, the figure is 46%. These are views on capital availability, not financing rejection rates. Even so, they put a limit on how much optimism developers should take from a recovery in dealmaking.

Cheaper or more available debt helps. The developer still needs an investor willing to fund the rest.

Canadian respondents were more likely to expect an undersupply of development/redevelopment equity capital (63%) than debt capital (46%) in 2027. These are survey expectations, not measured financing volumes. Source: PwC and ULI, Emerging Trends in Real Estate 2027, pp. 136–137. Original chart.

More deals do not necessarily mean more construction

Canadian commercial real estate investment reached $16.2 billion in the second quarter of 2026, according to the CBRE figures cited in the report. That was the strongest quarter since early 2022. The total includes mergers and acquisitions, so a few large transactions can do a lot of the lifting. It tells us money is moving again, without telling us how broadly the recovery has spread.

There is also a practical reason an investor might buy an existing building before funding a new one. An occupied property already collects rent. A development can spend years consuming cash before the first tenant moves in.

The buyer of an existing building can negotiate the price down. A developer has to work with the cost of delivering a new one. Construction and servicing bills don't fall just because the building down the street sold at a discount.

That leaves room for a busy acquisitions market and a weak construction market at the same time. Investors can buy assets from struggling owners without financing the next round of projects.

Some of those sales will help. A new owner may have the cash to finish a stalled building, or a lower purchase price may finally make the numbers work. The test is whether construction follows the transaction.

Toronto is already starting fewer homes

The report puts Toronto census metropolitan area housing starts at 26,087 in 2025, down from 37,718 in 2024, citing CMHC. That is 11,631 fewer homes started in a year, a decline of about 31%. These are historical construction starts, not a prediction of how many homes will be finished in 2027.

Toronto census metropolitan area housing starts fell from 37,718 units in 2024 to 26,087 in 2025, a 30.8% decline (rounded to 31%). Starts measure construction begun, not completed homes. Source: CMHC, as cited in PwC and ULI, Emerging Trends in Real Estate 2027, p. 145. Original chart.

A thinner construction pipeline gives developers a reason to expect less competition when their buildings open. It can be a sound argument for buying a site. It is a much harder argument to make to an investor who needs their money back before the project is ready.

In the meantime, the carrying costs keep coming.

A partner willing to wait through a slow lease-up gives a project more room than one counting on an early sale. Both can believe Toronto needs more housing. They still need to agree on how long they can afford to wait for the income.

A rental conversion needs a new business plan

The report describes continued long-term interest in purpose-built rental. Some interviewees are much less convinced that today's rents can cover the cost of building and financing it. Both views can be reasonable.

Changing a condo proposal to rental means rewriting the business plan. The developer gives up the expected proceeds from individual suite sales and collects rent over years instead. The design and financing have to support that longer commitment, including the cost of running the building.

Start with the rent a tenant will actually pay. If a competing building offers free months, its advertised rent overstates what the landlord collects over that lease. Using that advertised rent as a comparable can overstate the income the new project will collect.

Then check how long it will take to fill the building. Reaching the target rent six months late can still leave the owner short of cash. The partners need to know who covers that shortfall before the first bill arrives.

The next equity cheque may go into an old building

Loans coming due in 2027 will compete for that money too. PwC and ULI describe owners using preferred equity, mezzanine financing and joint ventures to close funding gaps.

If a replacement loan is smaller than the debt being repaid, the borrower has to make up the difference. That can mean putting cash into a building they already own instead of buying the next site.

The terms deserve as much attention as the amount raised. Preferred returns and fees can leave less income for the original owner. Repayment deadlines can force decisions well before that owner intended to sell. A refinancing that solves today's shortage may leave very little room for the next delay.

Before committing more money, a developer should know which assumption the project can least afford to get wrong. If a small rent reduction or a few extra months of vacancy wipes out the return, a higher exit value in the spreadsheet is doing too much work.

Housing policy has to deal with those gaps too. A fee reduction helps if it brings the cost within reach of the revenue a project can earn. A financing program helps if it supplies money on terms the project can carry. The evidence of success is a financed project that starts construction.

The report gives developers a reason to call investors again. Those calls still have to end with an agreement on the equity and how long it can stay in the project. Until then, a recovery in transactions offers limited comfort to the owner paying to hold an empty site.

items.title: Budget 2026 shifts Liberal government's language on home construction targets
items.description: OTTAWA — The federal housing minister's office is reasserting Ottawa's goal of doubling the pace of home construction — even though references to the Liberals' hallmark affordability pledge were missing from Budget 2026.
items._ogDesc: OTTAWA — The federal housing minister's office is reasserting Ottawa's goal of doubling the pace of home construction — even though references to the Liberals' hallmark affordability pledge were missing from Budget 2026.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The federal housing minister's office is reasserting Ottawa's goal of doubling the pace of home construction — even though references to the Liberals' hallmark affordability pledge were missing from Budget 2026.

The budget, which was tabled last week, dropped any mention of that original target, which was introduced in the Liberals' 2025 election platform and repeated numerous times in that year's budget.

Instead, the 511-page document outlines a new plan to triple the pace of non-market housing construction to 24,000 starts per year over the next decade.

Non-market housing is usually more affordable and relies on government support to get built, but those homes account for only a small share of the overall number of units built in a year.

The Canadian Press asked Housing Minister Gregor Robertson's office whether Ottawa is abandoning its goal of doubling the annual pace of overall home building.

After repeated requests, his office pointed to a six-month-old statement given to The Canadian Press in May confirming that the government was still "working toward doubling homebuilding over the next decade."

At the time, The Canadian Press had asked Robertson's office about Ottawa's commitment to the target because April's spring economic update also lacked references to the goal.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan pointed out then that while the government's fiscal update included plenty of talk about affordability supports, "no specific targets or metrics for the pace of home building were provided."

Housing affordability has been a hot-button issue since the COVID-19 pandemic, which saw rents and resale prices rapidly escalate — boxing out many young Canadians trying to become homeowners.

On Tuesday, Robertson's office pointed to statistics showing national housing starts are up more than 20 per cent since the pre-pandemic period, rental construction is setting a record pace and rents have trended lower over the past few years.

"Since forming government, we launched an ambitious national plan to focus our efforts and spur co-ordinated action between governments, homebuilders, and communities. We moved quickly to increase housing supply and improve access to safe, warm, affordable homes," his office said.

MP Scott Aitchison, the Conservative housing critic, accused the Liberals of quietly dropping the promise to double home building and replacing it with the smaller non-market target.

"Their announcements and promises have turned into another Liberal housing illusion. Tripling the speed of slow is still unbearably slow and will not restore affordability," Aitchison said in a statement to The Canadian Press.

"Canadians need homes they can afford, not more failed Liberal targets and broken promises.”

In its fall housing supply report, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. wrote that the country is entering a "new phase" where slowing population growth is leading to more balance in Canadian rental markets.

But the Crown corporation warned that the annual pace of housing starts is well short of levels needed to restore pre-pandemic affordability to the market in the next 10 years.

The CMHC's "business-as-usual" forecast sees Canada breaking ground on 231,000 homes per year, which it estimates would leave the market up to 238,000 homes short of affordable levels by 2036.

Affordability will remain out of reach if Canada fails to take advantage of this moment to rapidly build housing supply ahead of the next surge in demand, the CMHC said.

Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Missing Middle Institute, said he always viewed the Liberals' goal of doubling home building levels as a tough one to achieve. It would mean bringing the annual number of housing starts up to 500,000 in a given year, when Canada has so far topped out around 300,000.

Moffatt said the target may also be "excessive," given that the government can effectively control the pace of population growth, which dictates how much supply is really needed to serve the Canadian market.

The headline number also doesn't specify what kinds of homes Canada needs to build to actually meet Canadians' needs, he added.

"I never loved the target. I felt it was probably too high and missed some important nuances," Moffatt said.

The federal Liberals have instituted a number of policy changes aimed at stimulating home building since Prime Minister Mark Carney came to office in March 2025.

They include waiving the GST on many newly built homes, establishing new funds for local infrastructure and setting up Build Canada Homes, a new Crown corporation tasked with reversing years of lagging non-market home construction.

Budget 2026 proposed giving another $13 billion over 10 years to Build Canada Homes and pledged tens of billions of dollars over the coming decade to an effort to end homelessness across the country.

Andy Yan, director of the City Program at Simon Fraser University, also said he considered Ottawa's original home building goal "more aspirational than realistic."

"You can set a target, but do you have the capacity to meet those targets?" he said.

Yan said policies like the Housing Accelerator Fund and the Apartment Construction Loan Program have been "fairly successful" in getting more homes built, particularly on the rental side.

The Housing Accelerator Fund, which ties federal cash to pro-development policy changes, was one of Ottawa's tools for addressing the fact that barriers to building often lie at the municipal level.

Many of the other levers for stimulating home building are also not directly in the federal government's hands.

Building material costs have grown in response to U.S. tariffs, while a soft labour market is dampening buyer demand for new homes.

Interest rates — a critical factor for developers weighing the business case for a new build — are set independently by the Bank of Canada. The central bank delivered its first rate hike in more than three years last month and signalled more could be on the way.

Moffatt warned that many of the constraints holding back broader construction apply to social housing as well.

"There's no non-market drywall, right? There's no non-market lumber, there's no non market electrician," he said.

"A non-market social housing target is more in the government's control, but it's hardly a slam dunk."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: BMO sees Canada’s immigration changes doubling expected population growth in 2027, keeping housing demand higher as more temporary residents stay.
items.body:
Canada’s continuing its immigration experiments but this time it’s a little more discreet. Ottawa’s 2027-29 immigration plan maintains the current regular permanent resident admissions target. However, BMO notes that existing and new special measures mean the number of permanent residents will be much higher. As a result, the bank’s economists have nearly doubled their population growth forecast.

Canada’s Immigration Measures Lift Effective Target To 660,000

Ottawa’s immigration target may look conservative, but it’s much bigger than the fragmented announcements suggest. The 2027-2029 immigration plan maintains 380,000 admissions annually, but BMO projects the target is actually much higher than the headline numbers suggest.

“While Ottawa maintains permanent resident targets of 380k per year, special one-time measures (from both the 2025 and 2026 budgets) build significantly on that amount,” explains BMO senior economist Robert Kavcic.

Canada Hopes To Attract A Lot More Permanent Residents

Permanent residents: actual admissions, target admissions, and special measures.

Source: BMO Capital Markets; StatCan; Budget 2026.

He notes that special measures in Budget 2025 and 2026 add roughly 280,000 temporary-to-permanent resident transitions in 2027. “In other words, roughly 280k temporary residents will be granted permanent resident status in 2027, with officials suggesting this will be on top of new admissions,” says Kavcic. After the special measures, BMO puts the total closer to 660,000 permanent residents.

BMO Sees Population Growth Rebounding To Nearly 1% In 2027

The measures mean population growth is seen bouncing much higher than previously forecast. BMO now expects the population to expand roughly 1% in 2027, nearly double the 0.5% they previously anticipated. “In effect, because those temporary residents are now not leaving, they will not drag on population growth as previously expected,” explains Kavcic.

The special measures largely aim to keep people already in the country. Converting their status won’t immediately add housing demand, but fewer departures would mean fewer homes freed up for the temporary resident inflow. This reduced churn can boost housing demand more than previously anticipated, even without changing the headline immigration target.

“This is an abrupt change in the near-term outlook,” says Kavcic, questioning whether repeated one-time measures make planning harder for the Bank of Canada, homebuilders, and municipalities.

Since housing takes years to build, the read is that policymakers are trying to overshoot supply with further demand stimulus. However, the state of the Canadian economy is very different from last time it was attempted. With Canadians leaving in record volumes to find opportunities elsewhere, the ability to retain and attract immigrants may be harder than simply raising a quota.

items.title: What brokers need to know about an ever-evolving appraisal process
items.description: Appraisal executive emphasizes key differences in the alternative space
items.content: <p>Appraisal executive emphasizes key differences in the alternative space</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639299368595742752.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Appraisal executive emphasizes key differences in the alternative space
items.body:
Canadian mortgage brokers have established themselves as a key conduit between borrowers and lenders – but in the alternative lending space, that role expands to becoming the connector between borrower, lender, and appraiser.

That fact means it’s doubly important for brokers in the sector to take the time to understand what appraisers do and why they do it, according to Appraisal Institute of Canada (AIC) director Claudio Polito (pictured top). 

Among the main misconceptions about an appraiser’s role, Polito told Canadian Mortgage Professional, is that an appraisal is simply a property value. “To most people – the borrower, the broker, perhaps even the lender – the value is the most important part,” he said. “But to the appraiser, the value is just a component of it. There’s a story to be told.”

That story includes neighbourhood context, physical improvements, and market activity – all of which feed into the final opinion of value. Polito also pointed out that lender requirements vary considerably, and brokers should factor this into their preparation.

“Brokers are asked to know their client and we’re asking them to know their lender as well,” he said. “A Big Five bank may have one requirement. A private lending individual may have a different requirement. Even within the same space, there are different requirements.”

Polito’s main advice for brokers is on client preparation, an area he said too many brokers overlook until problems arise. His recommendation: get ahead of potential issues by asking the right questions early.

“Rather than having the appraiser highlight potential areas of concern, have the broker be made aware of that first,” he said. “Do you have a basement apartment? Is it registered? Is it approved by the municipality? Do you have an addition? Was it done with or without permits? These are questions the appraiser will ask – better we know up front.”

What’s changed in the current market

In the current climate, expectation management on value is equally important – especially because of the significant drop in values across many markets since the peak of 2021 and 2022. The borrowers who purchased at the height of the market sometimes carry expectations that no longer reflect reality, according to Polito.

“If you purchased your property in Toronto in 2022 for $1 million and you’re asking for a home line of credit and thinking the property is worth $1.5 million, what makes you think the property has gone up half a million dollars when everything in the news says the Toronto market is declining?” he said.

The condo market has suffered an especially noteworthy downturn, leading to appraisal challenges as buyers who purchased preconstruction units are suddenly unable to secure a mortgage for the amount they agreed to buy the property for years back.

How AI is impacting the appraisal process

Another big trend to impact the appraisals space in recent years, unsurprisingly, has been artificial intelligence (AI). The rise of AI-driven property valuations is having a big say on how some borrowers, and even some lenders, approach the question of what a property is worth.

Polito still believes AI will never completely eradicate the human influence from the appraisal process. “AI can be a great tool when it’s properly applied with guardrails in place, when there’s the human element and the human involvement in it,” he said.

“But you’re seeing more and more homeowners and borrowers relying on AI – and that could be dangerous. It could lead to false expectations, either overstated or understated.”

On automated valuation models (AVMs), increasingly used by lenders in lower-risk transactions, Polito is also sceptical whether their influence will ultimately threaten the human factor.

“Take those with a grain of salt, knowing that what a platform spits out may not be completely accurate in the same way that what a professional appraiser might conclude the property is worth,” he said.

“An appraiser uses all of their senses as part of the analysis. An appraiser sees what the analytical computer doesn’t see.”
