TORONTO — The average asking price for a rental unit across Canada in October was $2,036, down 3.2 per cent compared with a year ago. 
 A monthly report from Rentals.
items._ogDesc: TORONTO — The average asking price for a rental unit across Canada in October was $2,036, down 3.2 per cent compared with a year ago. A monthly report from Rentals.
items.body:
TORONTO — The average asking price for a rental unit across Canada in October was $2,036, down 3.2 per cent compared with a year ago.

A monthly report from Rentals.ca and Urbanation says October's decrease marks the smallest year-over-year decline since February, when rents were down 2.8 per cent from the same month a year earlier.

Average asking rents have now fallen year-over-year for 25 consecutive months, with prices down 5.4 per cent compared with two years ago and reaching their lowest October level since 2022.

Rents were essentially flat on a monthly basis, edging 0.1 per cent higher from September.

Urbanation president Shaun Hildebrand says the window for cheaper rents is closing in Toronto and Vancouver as prices are starting to rise for the first time in nearly three years amid declining supply, while renters still hold the advantage in Calgary, Edmonton and much of Ontario, where prices continue to fall.

Asking rents for purpose-built apartments fell 2.1 per cent year-over-year to an average of $2,040 last month, while asking rents for condominium apartments decreased 5.5 per cent to $2,048.

items.title: Lower Prices Softening The Hit Of Higher Borrowing Costs For GTA Buyers
items.description:
Borrowing costs in the Greater Toronto Area are higher than they were a year ago.

Even so, the monthly mortgage payment on an average-priced home has only edged up, and it’s still well below what buyers were paying in 2023 and 2024, according to the latest from the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board (TRREB).

“GTA homebuyers continued to benefit from substantial negotiating power on price over the past year. While borrowing costs have increased on the back of higher inflation, the impact on monthly mortgage payments has been mitigated by lower selling prices, helping keep affordability in check,” said TRREB Chief Information Officer Jason Mercer.

Prices have continued to fall from last year’s levels. In October, the MLS® Home Price Index (MLS® HPI) Composite benchmark was 4.3% lower than a year earlier. The average selling price came in at $1,024,108, down 2.7%.

Even with lower prices, many buyers are still holding back. TRREB says they’re uncertain about where inflation, borrowing costs and the economy are headed.

There were 5,603 home sales through TRREB’s MLS® System in October, 7.9% fewer than in October 2025. New listings dropped to 14,173, down 11.9% year-over-year.

The month-to-month picture looks different. With seasonal adjustment, sales, new listings, the HPI Composite and the average selling price all moved up from September.

TRREB President Daniel Steinfeld said a clearer economic picture could bring buyers back in the new year.

“If a Canada-U.S. trade deal is reached, GTA residents could gain a clearer picture of the economic outlook. Combined with a resolution to the conflict in the Middle East, this could help ease concerns about inflation and economic uncertainty, strengthen consumer confidence and renew interest in homeownership as we move into 2027,” said Steinfeld.

TRREB CEO John DiMichele took a longer view.

“While we continue to experience shorter-term volatility in the ownership housing market, we can’t lose track of the fact that the permanent population will continue to grow in our region. Policy announcements, including HST rebates and development charge reductions should help bring a greater diversity of ownership and rental supply online in the medium-term to ensure new families are properly and affordably housed,” said DiMichele.

items.title: Housing experts urge B.C. to rethink development charges
items.description: U.S., U.K., Australia offer different approaches to paying for infrastructure
items._ogDesc: U.S., U.K., Australia offer different approaches to paying for infrastructure
items.body:
With Metro Vancouver condo construction hitting a 15-year low amid rising costs and slower demand, some housing experts and developers say it may be time to revisit development charges and consider alternative ways to fund municipal infrastructure.

Development charges are fees municipalities levy on developers when they build new homes or other projects. The money helps pay for infrastructure needed to support new development, such as roads, water and sewer pipes, drainage, parks and community facilities.

However, what were originally modest charges have increased “at an alarming rate” in many Canadian municipalities, including in B.C., according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).

“It started as an earmarked tax that is very focused and determined on a specific purpose. But over time what happened is they started to fund more and more different purposes,” said Mathieu Laberge, chief economist at CMHC.

“[Development charges] now in some centres are used to fund public libraries, firefighting services or police services, daycare.”

A 2023 report by the Urban Development Institute found that government taxes and fees, including development charges, can account for about 29 per cent of the purchase price of a new condo unit in Vancouver.

“Ultimately it's embedded in the price of new homes and it's passed on to buyers,” said Laberge.

In June, Ontario and the federal government launched an $8.8-billion development charge reduction program. Participating municipalities must commit to reducing development charges by at least 30-50 per cent for three years, and federal and provincial funding helps replace some lost municipal revenue.

Michael Waters, CEO of Ottawa-based Minto Group, which has multiple projects under construction in B.C., said he believes similar initiatives are needed in B.C. to help lower building costs and encourage more development.

“Voters get a property tax bill every year. They can see the rate at which their property taxes have gone up,” said Waters.

“It's not as apparent what development charges are or how the rate at which they climbed from year to year. And so they don't typically attract the same level of scrutiny in municipal politics.”

Alternative funding models

Revisiting development charges raises questions about their role in funding municipal infrastructure and how municipalities would make up any shortfall if the fees were reduced.

Andrew Sancton, professor emeritus of political science at Western University, said the “old-fashioned way” is for municipalities to borrow money to build new infrastructure projects, then pay those loans back through property taxes collected or utility charges.

“In most places, the cost of new infrastructure is paid for by everybody, not by just the people who are purchasing new buildings,” he said. “And development charges have replaced that method in many ways.”

For example, if a new wastewater plant is needed in a developing area, a municipality could borrow the money to build it and it will be paid back over time through revenue from users of the system, Sancton said.

He pointed to tax increment financing. Under this model, a municipality can finance an infrastructure project upfront and repay the debt using increases in property-tax revenue generated within a designated area as it develops.

Waters said other countries have adopted different mechanisms to funding growth-related infrastructure that could inspire some ideas for B.C.

In England, some local authorities use the Community Infrastructure Levy, a charge on eligible new development that helps fund infrastructure needed to support growth. Some U.S. municipalities use special district financing, issuing bonds to cover upfront infrastructure costs and repaying them through taxes or assessments on properties within designated areas.

In New South Wales, Australia, a standardized Housing and Productivity Contribution helps fund state and regional infrastructure, including major roads, public transit, schools and hospitals, while municipalities continue to collect separate contributions for local infrastructure.

“I'm not saying any of these are a silver bullet or a way that you can replace [development charges] entirely, but could they be used to complement or, in concert with development charges, to make the sharing of infrastructure costs more equitable?” said Waters.

Quebec and Alberta are using a different tax mix instead of development charges, according to Laberge. For example, Quebec municipalities can borrow money and issue municipal bonds to finance capital projects, including infrastructure.

But Laberge noted that even if development charges are reduced significantly or even eliminated, it wouldn't be sufficient to resolve the supply gap observed across the province.

“Other things need to be done as well, and other factors involved. We need to look at development charges, but also more broadly, red tape and how we build.”

items.title: Victoria's Market Square is on the market for $25M
items.description: The collection of heritage buildings around an open-air courtyard is on half a city block bordered by Pandora Avenue, Store Street and Johnson Street.
items._ogDesc: The collection of heritage buildings around an open-air courtyard is on half a city block bordered by Pandora Avenue, Store Street and Johnson Street.
items.body:
A prime 1.5-acre swath of downtown Victoria is on the market for $25 million.

Market Square, a collection of heritage buildings around an open-air courtyard on half a city block bordered by Pandora Avenue, Store Street and Johnson Street, was listed for sale this week.

The owners, Vancouver-based Anthem Properties, acquired the property more than 20 years ago.

Commercial real estate agent Matt Pettinger said a number of groups have expressed interest in acquiring Market Square.

“Market Square is one of those properties that almost everyone in the Victoria area is familiar with,” said Pettinger, a senior vice-president with Avison Young. “Opportunities to acquire an asset of this profile in the downtown core don’t come along very often.”

Market Square was established in the 1970s by brothers Sam and Nick Bawlf.

The project, according to Canada’s Historic Places, was an attempt to reactivate a depressed downtown core and breathe new life into historic buildings, including the Milne Block in the 500-block of Johnson Street that was built in 1891.

All of the buildings were built between 1890 and 1912 and the property covers just under 1.5 acres.

There is a total leasable space of more than 95,000 square feet, including 56,775 square feet of retail space and 38,658 square feet of office space.

Less than 10 per cent of the total leasable space is currently vacant, Pettinger said, adding most of that is office space.

The square provides a net operating income of $1.94 million annually, and includes Famoso Italian Pizzeria, Café Mexico, The Drake Eatery, Whistle Buoy Brewing and Pacific Rim College as its major tenants.

Pettinger said any potential buyers will have to sign a non-disclosure agreement to get access to information on leases and other details.

Market Square is the second high-profile stretch of the downtown to hit the market this fall.

In September, the two-storey Broad Street Square at 1290 Broad St. was listed for sale, with an asking price of $10.95 million.

The 25,000-square-foot building occupies half of the 1200-block on the west side of Broad Street and a long stretch of the 600-block of Yates Street.

items.title: New hotel design pitched for burned Plaza site in downtown Victoria
items.description: Tech company Redbrick has unveiled its plan for a 198-room, 17-storey hotel at the corner of Government Street and Pandora Avenue.
items._ogDesc: Tech company Redbrick has unveiled its plan for a 198-room, 17-storey hotel at the corner of Government Street and Pandora Avenue.
items.body:
The new owner of the downtown Victoria property where a massive fire destroyed the Plaza Hotel seven years ago is taking another run at building a new hotel on the site.

Victoria tech company Redbrick unveiled its designs this week for a 198-room, 17-storey hotel at the corner of Government Street and Pandora Avenue.

The Plaza burned to the ground on May 6, 2019, in a blaze determined to have been sparked by arson.

The high-profile site across from the McPherson Playhouse, Centennial Square and city hall has remained vacant behind a high plywood wall ever since, despite an effort by another developer to build a hotel on the property.

A proposal for a 12-storey, 200-room hotel was declined by Victoria city council last year, on the grounds that the proposed height and density didn’t fit in with the neighbourhood.

Oceangate Developments and Mairet Hotels said in January that it had lost confidence that the project could proceed, and sold the property to Redbrick for an undisclosed amount.

Redbrick chief executive Tobyn Sowden said the new plan is for a heritage-style four-storey podium structure that would fit in with neighbouring Old Town buildings, topped by a floor for an indoor and outdoor spa, then a 12-storey tower.

The total height of the proposed building is 64.5 metres, including a rooftop restaurant and bar with a view of the harbour.

Sowden said the hotel still needs about 200 rooms to be viable, but the podium design would make it a better fit within the neighbourhood, which is largely made up of two- and three-storey buildings.

The glass tower, meanwhile, would be set back off Government Street, “so you don’t feel that sheer height as you’re walking as a pedestrian alongside a historic-style podium.”

An open house at Redbrick’s Douglas Street headquarters on Tuesday and a new website are the first steps in gathering public feedback before the company takes its proposal to city council, likely by the end of the year.

Redbrick is partnering with Victoria builder Aryze and Seattle-based architect Olson Kundig on the project, which includes a plaza courtyard on city-owned land with widened sidewalks, pedestrian walkways, seating and landscaping. The project also includes a spa with outdoor gardens along the podium’s second floor, and four levels of underground parking.

Sowden is calling it the Westholme after the lumber company that built the original hotel on the site in 1911.

The Westholme Hotel was one of Victoria’s largest hotels at the time, with a 600-seat dining room and a dance floor with room for an orchestra. The building had numerous other names and uses over the years, including as a country and western bar and one of the city’s last strip clubs.

Sowden said Westholme built the hotel to diversify from its lumber business, and Redbrick is essentially doing the same by rebuilding a hotel in the same neighbourhood where he has built his own business over the last 15 years.

Sowden called the proposed hotel a “gateway” to the industry, arts and innovation district the city is developing at the north end of downtown. Residential development is planned around the Capital Iron lands, and the Art Gallery of Greater Victoria could eventually move into the area.

“It’s going to push commerce further down Government Street,” said Sowden. “We want it to be that connection to Chinatown and have tourists go further while at the same time having locals make it their destination, like see a show at the McPherson and having a bite or a drink at the Westholme.”

Sowden said the proposal also responds to a critical need for visitor accommodations, with the region’s hotel supply having dropped nearly 25% since 2016.

The Greater Victoria Hotel Development Working Group estimates that 2,000 net new hotel rooms will be needed over the next decade. The city’s Official Community Plan is targeting 1,500 new hotel rooms by 2035.

items.title: Repealing B.C. housing legislation would be a mistake, says UBC expert
items.description: VICTORIA — A glut of empty condos in British Columbia should not be seen as evidence that the market is working, said a housing expert who warned against winding back policies of the outgoing NDP government designed to tame prices and rent.
items._ogDesc: VICTORIA — A glut of empty condos in British Columbia should not be seen as evidence that the market is working, said a housing expert who warned against winding back policies of the outgoing NDP government designed to tame prices and rent.
items.body:
VICTORIA — A glut of empty condos in British Columbia should not be seen as evidence that the market is working, said a housing expert who warned against winding back policies of the outgoing NDP government designed to tame prices and rent.

Alexandra Flynn, who teaches housing policy at the University of B.C., said the province still needs a lot of homes for low-to very-low-income residents, despite the thousands of empty units.

"We do have a number of empty condos, but market housing for above-average income earners is not the housing we need," she said. Left alone, the market cannot supply affordable and deeply affordable housing, she added.

"If you asked any developer, they would tell you, absent some kind of government intervention and granting and funding, they are not going to be able to do it."

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has promised to repeal key aspects of the provincial housing legislation introduced by the outgoing government of Premier David Eby.

"We will return housing decisions to the people and the communities, who know their neighbourhoods so much better than Victoria," Doerkson said during the inaugural meeting of the Conservative caucus.

Doerkson was referring to the proposed repeal of Bill 44, which New Democrats consider their signature piece of housing legislation.

The legislation legalized higher densities on single-lot properties in municipalities with populations above 5,000 people, but also came with housing targets, which have been heavily criticized by local governments.

Sarrah Storey, president of the Union of the British Columbia Municipalities, said Bill 44 was "highly problematic" and municipalities pushed back because the government imposed it as a "one-size-fits-all model" without getting input.

Storey said UBCM agrees with the idea that housing policy for Williams Lake should not be made in Victoria, but if government wants to make changes to Bill 44, it should give municipalities choice.

"There are some local governments that will want to remain with the policies that are in place, allowing multiple homes on single family lots, for example, and they should be able to do so," she said.

Storey, who is the mayor for Fraser Lake, said any housing plan must also consider infrastructure needs.

"I say the best way to support developers is to ensure that the local governments can direct development to areas that are ready to support growth," she said.

Flynn disagrees with the plan to repeal, saying the law can be a "powerful tool," and while some of it needs to be fixed, it would be a mistake to just throw it away.

"If I was the new government, I would not be making any knee-jerk reactions right now," she said.

Flynn said she understands criticism from municipalities, saying there was "no question" that the dialogue between municipalities and Victoria must be improved.

"The province should not be dictating what municipalities do without actually engaging and having the bilateral relationships that are appropriate," Flynn said.

She said housing in British Columbia is in a better place now than it was in 2017 for lots of reasons.

They include the work of the non-profit housing sector, municipalities, the federal government, and the provincial government, she said.

"So, the NDP government introduced some of the most transformative housing reforms in Canada," she said.

Changing circumstances over time do not negate the fact that municipalities need to ensure affordable housing can be built in their communities, she said.

"This is not the time to be thinking about what to repeal," she said. "It's a time to set the course for a new agenda moving forward."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

Wolfgang Depner, The Canadian Press

items.description:
VANCOUVER — The home on Windsor Street in East Vancouver has admittedly seen better days. 
 Its yard is overgrown, the weathered shingles are barely hanging on in places, and the back stairs have completely disintegrated.
items._ogDesc: VANCOUVER — The home on Windsor Street in East Vancouver has admittedly seen better days. Its yard is overgrown, the weathered shingles are barely hanging on in places, and the back stairs have completely disintegrated.
items.body:
VANCOUVER — The home on Windsor Street in East Vancouver has admittedly seen better days.

Its yard is overgrown, the weathered shingles are barely hanging on in places, and the back stairs have completely disintegrated.

But with an official BC Assessment valuation of more than $1.7 million, the house appeared to represent a bargain when it sold for $825,000 at Vancouver's annual tax auction at city hall on Wednesday. It had a reserve price of just $72,051.

It was among more than 60 properties auctioned off in this year's City of Vancouver tax sale, set off by owners who have not paid their taxes for three years in a row, with the reserve, or upset prices, set at the amounts owed to the city.

If East Vancouver is not to your taste, then perhaps Point Grey Road? It's one of the most exclusive addresses in Canada, where neighbours include Lululemon billionaire Chip Wilson, whose $73-million home is the most valuable in B.C.

A few blocks down the road from Wilson are two side-by-side houses valued around $5 million and $6 million. They are steps from Jericho Beach and the Royal Vancouver Yacht Club, and sold for less than half their values at $2 million and $2.75 million respectively.

There is, of course, a catch.

After auction day, the current owners have a year to redeem their property by paying their taxes, resulting in a refund to the bidder — plus interest at the rate of six per cent, far in excess of government bond yields or bank interest.

Ron Usher, a retired notary public, said tax auctions are "not for the faint of heart or the inexperienced."

"I suspect some of these tax sales are more whoops than deliberate," Usher said, citing situations such as inheritances.

"You can imagine the law is very much structured to give the maximum possible opportunity for the owner to sort out the problem," Usher said.

Though a posting last week included 116 properties listed for auction, by the time it began at 10 a.m. Wednesday, only 66 remained. Owners of three more properties paid their taxes while the auction was ongoing and the homes were removed from the block.

Vancouverite Darius Wu attended the auction "mostly for fun, hoping I'd get a bargain."

The 30-year-old likened the auction to buying a lottery ticket, but better.

"In a lottery, you lose money no matter what. Here, I would say, the odds are probably one in a hundred. You don't lose any money, and if you win, it's still … pretty good."

It was Wu's first auction in Vancouver, but he ducked out before noon after concluding he wouldn't outbid others in attendance.

"I think there are way more serious people here," he said, noting many of the bids were climbing to around half of the property value listed. "You need a lot of cash to actually participate here."

As the auction dragged on, most of those who earlier jockeyed for a spot inside the chambers trickled out, with the attendees dwindling to about a dozen.

Among them was a man who cast winning bids on dozens of properties, including the home on Windsor Street. Though he declined an interview, he said he didn't expect to be transferred the properties — he would instead collect the interest.

Winning bids are secured by paying the upset price. If the original owner pays their overdue tax within a year, the bidder is refunded the upset price with interest of six per cent. But if it is not redeemed after a year, the bidder takes ownership after paying the balance of their bid within 30 days.

Sean Holden, a longtime Vancouver Realtor, called bidding at the auction "an exercise in futility."

He said he often steers clients away from the auction. When asked if he has ever attended himself, his response is quick.

"I wouldn't waste my time," he said through a chuckle.

Holden points out that tax auction sales that go through to completion are very rare.

But they do happen, both in Vancouver and other B.C. municipalities that conduct their auctions every September on properties with two years of unpaid taxes.

Three properties have changed hands in the last five years in Burnaby, while the City of Vancouver said in a statement that there "were only three instances in the last 10 years where a property changed hands from a tax sale."

"The property taxes on almost all properties have historically been paid within the one-year redemption period," the statement said.

The City of Vancouver tells potential buyers not to trespass, but recommends people do their own research before bidding, noting in a posting last week that it is not responsible for the condition or quality of the homes.

"Prospective purchasers are urged to research the properties and make all necessary inquiries to municipal and other government departments to determine the existence of any bylaws, restriction, charges or other conditions which may affect the value or suitability of the properties," it says.

Holden, who has been a Realtor in the city for about three decades, said that adds risk for the buyer.

"You don't know what condition it will be, and (if) the sellers are forced out by the bank, whether they knock holes in the wall or do other strange things. You're taking a huge risk," he said.

All properties auctioned on Wednesday received bids. Only one property was sold for the upset price, but that amounted to nearly $1 million.

The two properties listed for sale in Burnaby last year both went through to completion.

The minutes from the tax sale show the same person purchased both properties.

An empty 9,262-square-foot lot on Walker Avenue sold for the upset price of $845, while its assessed value is $37,700.

The other property, which had an upset price of $269, was sold to the same buyer for $5,000. That may be less of a bargain — the property measures just 94-square feet and has a valuation of $3,600.

The City of Burnaby confirmed both properties were transferred after the one-year redemption period expired.

The City of Kelowna said it had an average of "about three to four properties" sold at its auction over the past six years, but added that "actual transfers of ownership through this process are very rare."

"City staff recall the last transfer occurring around 2016/2017," a spokeswoman said in a statement.

Abbotsford did not auction any properties this year or in 2024, but in 2025, it had two properties on the block. One sale went through on what the city called "a small undeveloped piece of land."

The highest bidders from Wednesday's auction in Vancouver must pay the upset price by noon Thursday.

Holden said bidders need to be prepared for their money to be tied up for a while, noting that while a six per cent interest rate may be enticing, most owners end up paying their taxes.

"Certainly, it's a way to put pressure on people to pay those outstanding taxes, and that's basically the function of it, for what it's worth," he said.

That seems to be the case for the property on Windsor Street, where a man who identified himself as the owner exited the house, causing the entire structure to rattle as he closed the door.

The resident, who declined to give his name, said he was aware his home was going on the auction block.

The property was, he said, his family home, while acknowledging that its ramshackle condition made living there "a challenge."

But he brushed off any concern about it being sold out from under him.

"I have a year to pay it," he said of his tax bill.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

Brieanna Charlebois, The Canadian Press

items.title: Zonix’s 1,060-Unit Grand Park Markham Project Placed Under Receivership
items.description:
After being listed for sale last year, the sprawling Grand Park project in Markham, Ontario is now under receivership, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court.

The subject site of the project is a 14-lot land assembly consisting of 36, 38, 40, 42, 44, 46, and 48 Steeles Avenue East, plus 37, 39, 41, 43, 45, 47, and 49 Highland Park Boulevard. The 2.3-acre site is located on the eastern side of Dudley Avenue, about two blocks northeast from Centerpoint Mall.

The developer is Zonix, which has historically been a developer of low-density projects and is based out of 44 Steeles Avenue East, according to the company’s website. The Steeles properties are held under Zonix Homes Inc. while the Highland Park properties are held under Zonix Dudley Inc.

For the site, Zonix was previously planning 533 residential units across a 27-storey tower and a six-storey building, before sizing the proposal up to 1,060 residential units across a 40-storey tower and a 44-storey tower.

For the project, Zonix secured financing from Toronto-based real estate lender Cameron Stephens, with the two sides reaching a loan agreement in February 2024 for the principal amount of $24,000,000, split between an initial advance of $21,457,000 to refinance existing debt, and a secondary advance of $2,543,000 to fund the acquisition of 45 Highland Park Boulevard.

The Refinancing

According to Cameron Stephens, Zonix defaulted on the loan around April 2025 when the loan matured and the loan was not repaid. The lender then issued a formal demand for payment in May 2025, after which the two sides entered into a forbearance agreement that delayed enforcement until June 13, 2025, to give the developer the opportunity to refinance the loan.

Following the forbearance period, Zonix asked for a further forbearance and requested they subordinate their first-ranking mortgage to facilitate a refinancing transaction with Vector Financial, which would see at least $21,300,000 paid to Cameron Stephens, leaving a residual principal of $3,370,803 that would accrue interest at 15% per annum.

The three parties signed the subordination agreement on July 24, 2025, and Cameron Stephens also agreed to not enforce on their security unless it had provided at least 90 days notice to Vector. Cameron Stephens then received a payment of $21,331,563.20.

The forbearance was then extended to April 30, 2026, by which Zonix was required to repay the residual debt, but it failed to do so, thus defaulting on the forbearance agreement and loan. Cameron Stephens then issued a demand for payment in May 2026, claiming a debt of $4,127,781.92 with interest accruing at a daily rate of $1,692.79.

According to Cameron Stephens, Vector Financial also issued demands for payment in May 2026 after the borrowers failed to make required monthly interest payments. Vector was owed $24,314,359.30 as of May 4, 2026, with interest accruing at a daily rate of $7,611.81.

Cameron Stephens then initiated a receivership proceeding on May 28.

The Pending Sale

The project planned for 36-48 Steeles Avenue East and 37-49 Highland Park Boulevard in Markham. (Arcadis, Zonix Homes)

Concurrently, attempts were being made to sell the 36-48 Steeles Avenue East and 37-49 Highland Park Boulevard site, which was listed for sale last summer, as previously reported by STOREYS.

According to court documents, an agreement was signed on April 27, 2026 to sell the properties to 17767749 Canada Inc. — who would then assign the purchase to the De Shan Foundation Inc. — for $31,000,000, which was planning to redevelop the site into a long-term care facility. Court filings include a letter dated August 26 from Councillor of Ward 5 Andrew Keyes in support of the plan.

However, the agreement included a closing credit of $1,200,000 to the purchaser for costs and legal fees, meaning the effective purchase price was $29,800,000, which was not enough to repay both debts in full when including interest up to the expected closing date of the transaction — November 9.

The original due diligence period was scheduled to expire on June 17, but was extended to August 19, on which Zonix said the purchaser was working with BMO to secure financing. Because of the pending transaction, the hearing for Cameron Stephen’s receivership application kept getting pushed back.

The purchase agreement included a condition that the purchaser would secure financing by October 8. On that day, the purchaser requested a two-week extension, while maintaining the closing date, but the request was denied. In an affidavit dated October 9, Zonix President Reza Esfahany said “I completely understand and appreciate the frustration that is being faced by the Lenders. But this is not a situation where the Respondents have been ‘dragging their feet.’”

The Receivership

Cameron Stephens, however, had waited long enough.

“In light of the existing shortfall and the additional costs that remain to be quantified, there is a substantial risk that the Lenders will suffer a loss even if the APS ultimately closes,” said Cameron Stephens in filing dated October 13. “The anticipated deficiency will continue to increase the longer closing is delayed as legal fees, interest, and other enforcement costs continue to accrue.”

“Even assuming the [purchase agreement] ultimately closes on November 9, 2026, there remains no evidence that the Purchaser has obtained the necessary financing or that the transaction is capable of closing within the proposed timeframe. […] The Respondents have now had several months and three adjournments to complete a refinancing or sale transaction sufficient to satisfy the secured indebtedness. No payments have been made to Cameron Stephens during that period, interest continues to accrue, and the anticipated shortfall continues to grow.”

On October 15, the Ontario Superior Court granted the receivership order. There have been no further updates since then; it remains to be seen whether the sale will close as scheduled.

items._ogDesc: Greater Toronto real estate prices have plunged 28.4% from peak levels. Weak sales and high inventory keep the region in a buyer's market.
items.body:
Greater Toronto real estate prices have now seen the largest correction in history. That didn’t stop prices from slipping further in October, according to TRREB data. Lofty inventory and weak sales pushed prices down to their lowest level in almost 6 years.

Toronto Real Estate Prices Have Plunged 28.4% Since Peak

The price of a typical home across Greater Toronto.

Source: TRREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a home across Greater Toronto slipped 0.13% (-$1.2k) to $915,400 in October, 4.3% (-$40.8k) lower than last year. Home prices have plunged 28.4% (-$363.4k) since peaking in 2022. Even the sharpest correction in the region’s history has yet to wipe out pandemic gains though. Prices are back to December 2020 levels, though many would argue this is a modelling issue. Weak demand may confirm that, as buyers clearly don’t see this level as a “deal.”

Toronto Home Sales Fall To 3 Year Low

Greater Toronto home sales through the MLS.

Source: TRREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

Sales suffered another setback last month. TRREB reported 5,600 sales through the MLS in October, down 7.9% from last year. This is the second year to show a year-over-year drop in sales, marking a 3-year low for the month. Last month’s demand wasn’t the worst in the slump, but pre-pandemic volumes hadn’t been this low since 2008. Not the worst, but certainly far from anything that resembles normal.

Fewer New Listings, But The Volume Remains Historically Strong

New listings provided something for Toronto real estate bulls to chew on. There were 14,170 new listings in October, 11.9% lower than last year. The slide also marked the weakest October since 2022, though there’s no need to fear a shortage. Despite being the slowest volume for the month in 4 years, only 8 of the past 22 years have seen more new listings.

The sales-to-new-listings ratio (SNLR) only came in at 37.9% in October. That means TRREB is still in a buyer’s market, where the industry expects prices to fall further.

Toronto Real Estate Inventory Pulls Back, Third Highest On Record

Greater Toronto active listings of homes for sale in October.

Source: TRREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

One reason for the weak inflow of new listings may be the lofty levels of inventory sitting on the market. There were 25,100 active listings for sale in October, down 10% from last year but the third-most ever. The year-over-year drop was sharp, but it’s from the record high for October.

Greater Toronto real estate doesn’t look like it’s set to exit its tailspin soon. The prolonged correction is working at a snail’s pace, spending 4 years to roll back roughly 14 months of gains. With experts warning of higher rates and a wobbly economy, any mitigating factors seem beyond the horizon.

items.description:

An energy shortage? Nah, most don’t even apply for a connection to the power grid. This is about a little tax code change that sparked […]

The post The Data Center Boom: Internet Landlords & A $3 Trillion Real Estate Bubble appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: The scramble to build data centers isn't about AI, it's a $3 trillion real estate bubble as firms fight to become landlords of the internet.
items.body:
The AI revolution requires an unprecedented build-out of data centers. At least, that’s how the narrative goes. A quick peek at the data reveals a funny detail—most aren’t being built. An energy shortage? Nah, most don’t even apply for a connection to the power grid. This is about a little tax code change that sparked a stampede to become landlords of the internet. A multi-trillion dollar speculative bubble, complete with flippers. Seriously.

The Scramble To Build Data Centers

A scramble to build data centers is a bit of an understatement. In Canada, over 200 data centers have been announced or are in development. That includes 159 hyperscale facilities—those with at least 50 megawatts (MW) of capacity. Out of those, 116 are planning for over 100 MW of capacity. That’s a big jump from the 5 hyperscale facilities in Canada today.

The US is seeing a much bigger boom. Vancouver-based Aterio tracks 8,434 data centers, from announcement to operations. Their data shows 2,145 in operation, 888 under construction, and 4,442 announced. “The remaining 959 are delayed, land banked, not approved or cancelled, which we keep tracking because they often come back,” notes the predictive analytics firm.

If that seems unrealistic, wait until you crunch some numbers.

Data Center Energy Math Doesn’t Add Up

Big numbers are hard to appreciate, so let’s make them relatable. The average home in Canada and the US uses ~11,000 kilowatt hours (kWh) of electricity per year, about 1.25 kilowatts (kW). A megawatt (MW) is 1,000 kW, equal to the power draw of ~800 households. A gigawatt (GW) is 1,000,000 kW or 1,000 MW, equal to the power draw of ~800,000 households. Easy peasy, right?

Now let’s apply that. Canada’s 116 hyperscalers that need a minimum of 100 MW need 11.6 GW of power. That’s equal to the power of roughly 9.28 million households in a country with only ~16.85 million households. Canada’s Minister of Artificial Intelligence stated there are 20 GW in the pipeline.

Just 750 large projects in the US will be using 45 GW of additional power, equal to 36 million households. That’s a lot of automated Realtor emails for our spam boxes.

Does that sound a little unrealistic? Canada’s government seems to agree. When asked about the AI minister’s 20 GW claim, officials didn’t just concede it was an exaggeration. They outright stated, “most of this proposed capacity is not expected to proceed.”

Oh, cool. Wait… what? We’ll circle back, but first, let’s talk about the scramble to become landlords of the internet. That’s not me being cute. It’s in your tax code.

The Scramble To Become Landlords of The Internet

The internet is synonymous with giants like Google and Meta, but they’re mostly tenants. They’re now building data centers, but for the most part, they pay rent to “internet landlords,” a term coined by University of Maryland Associate Professor Daniel Greene.

“A tremendous amount of money and innovation may go into Google’s advertising networks, but those networks are largely housed in cages rented from a third party,” he explains.

He argues that internet landlords extract rent through three primary asset types: Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) for public network peering, co-location facilities where tenants rent space and server bandwidth, and managed storage. Internet companies may build products, but they have to rent infrastructure to get it to you.

One Weird Tax Trick That Ruined The Internet

This isn’t a happy accident but a long battle that only ended in 2016, which is why you’re hearing about it now. “To secure their status as [Real Estate Investment Trusts] REITs, internet landlords had to prove that the internet was a physical place you could own, manage, and lease, like an apartment building or a storage unit,” explains Greene.

IRS Private Letter Rulings (PLRs) from 2007 to 2014 helped to close gaps, including classifying payments as “rent.” The idea took off in 2015 after a PLR cleared the way for data center Equinix to become a Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT). Congress then codified the rules with the PATH Act (2015), and the IRS in 2016. Data centers were fully cleared to become tax-advantaged, globally traded, liquid financial assets.

What’s so important about being a REIT? Until the 1960s, real estate was incredibly illiquid, reducing its value. To stimulate investment, REITs became eligible for a pass-through structure. Corporate profits are usually subject to “double taxation.” They pay income taxes on net profits, and then they can pay out dividends from the profits. Investors then pay their own income taxes on that additional income. REITs distribute virtually the entire net profit as dividends, and investors pay income taxes on that income.

Roughly 10 years ago, the internet’s landlords secured the same treatment. It’s relatively new, which is why you’re only recently hearing about it. That and the recent rush to target retail investors with IPOs, such as Brookfield’s Csquare and Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC), the latter being a REIT itself.

On that note, let’s circle back to those data centers that are very unlikely.

Nearly 5 Data Centers Announced For Each Built & Braggawatts

The announcements (and debt) to build data centers are booming, but the building—not so much. In Canada, only 1 of 8 hyperscale facilities slated for a 2027 launch has actually broken ground. JP Morgan recently warned that over 60% of US data center capacity for 2027 hasn’t broken ground. Nearly 5 data centers are announced for every one built. That’s excluding cancelled projects.

The media widely attributes the delays to NIMBYs, who don’t want to share their energy. However, most data centers haven’t even asked for energy. A recent study of 252 active US data center announcements found 129 had no utility filings, SEC disclosures, or issued permits. That’s like announcing you’re going to bake a cake, but don’t have flour, sugar, an oven, or a kitchen.

Unproven and exaggerated data centers are so common that the industry has a term—braggawatts. These are, um, inspirational announcements with virtually zero chance of being built. “The amount of power, and even the amount of financing required to meet these upper end projections, it doesn’t exist,” explained Chris Sharp, CTO at Digital Realty, the firm that pioneered data REITs in 2004.

Sharp warns that developers are increasingly entering the space and overstating their abilities. Raw land of that scale is expensive. The cost to build out a hyperscale is almost unimaginable to most. Lucky for the speculators, they don’t need to build it if they can flip it first.

Data Center Flippers

Is it really a real estate bubble without flippers? A whopping 72% of US AI data center power requests are phantom loads. Phantom loads are speculative requests that require utility companies to set aside dedicated power. The artificial shortage pushes energy prices higher, but improves the project value. The flipper may not have the funds to build it out, but institutions that need to allocate investor funds do.

The problem isn’t going unnoticed. In Canada, B.C. Hydro now requires C$25k per MW in bid security, or C$2.5 million per 100 MW facility. Fail to build by the deadline, the funds are forfeited. It’s a little light in contrast to what’s emerging in the US.

Earlier this year, Texas adopted a US$100k study fee plus a deposit of US$50k per MW. A deposit of US$5 million is a sign of a pretty strong commitment. Though Ohio has the toughest test we’ve come across. Applicants pay US$10k-US$100k per load study, and 85% of contracted capacity for 12 years, even if less is used.

The scale of debt in the pipeline suggests that it may be an underreaction. Canada’s financing is more opaque, but experts have noted that debt raises “start at several hundred million dollars and exceed well over a billion dollars.” Though that’s chump change compared to the mounting liabilities in the US.

US data centers and related infrastructure are tied to US$1.3 trillion in debt, according to Atrium. Morgan Stanley also estimates a US$1.5 trillion “gap” in financing for data centers through 2028. Only the equivalent of Canada’s GDP? I guess we all have to tighten our purse strings in this economy.

AI has hit an inflection point, and that means more infrastructure is needed. But technological revolution and a bubble aren’t mutually exclusive. The internet was revolutionary, but that didn’t stop the Dot Com bubble. AI isn’t different—it’s just wrapped around a real estate bubble and cushioned by more tax dollars.

items.title: Expert: For Some, Homeownership Is Just A Dream
items.description:
For decades, buying a home was viewed as a rite of passage to adulthood. It represented stability, security, and the opportunity to build a future. Today, for many young people, it feels more like a fantasy than a realistic goal.

Recent polling and research have consistently shown that a growing number of young people no longer believe they will ever own a home. They don’t believe the housing crisis is being resolved.

While governments talk about affordability, youth do not see affordability improving in their daily lives.

Surveys of Ontarians aged 18 to 38 found that only 47% believe homeownership is achievable. More than one-quarter say it is not achievable at all, while another quarter are unsure. Young Ontarians are among the least optimistic people in Canada when it comes to their housing prospects.

A 2025 report commissioned by the Ontario Home Builders' Association found that young people in Ontario have "little hope" of buying a home. Eleven of 26 municipalities studied were deemed "completely unattainable" for middle-class households.

The report found that while house prices have more than doubled since 2005, inflation-adjusted wages have risen just 16%. In major markets such as Toronto, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, Guelph, and Barrie, homes now cost more than seven times annual pre-tax income.

Twenty-five years ago, the typical Ontario home cost roughly three to four times household income. Today, the ratio is closer to seven to nine times.

Not surprisingly, confidence has collapsed.

A housing outlook by the Ontario Real Estate Association (OREA) paints a similarly grim picture. Only 12% of Ontarians believe housing will become more affordable over the next five years. More than one-quarter of aspiring homeowners now believe they will never buy a home.

Young people are often accused of being pessimistic. In this case, however, their skepticism is justified.

This is not to say there haven’t been some positive developments.

Governments have finally acknowledged the severity of the housing crisis. The federal and Ontario governments have introduced new temporary HST rebates and other measures aimed at improving affordability while some municipalities have begun exploring reductions in development charges (DCs).

Polling conducted by Abacus Data for OREA found that 75% of Ontarians support reducing municipal DCs and 72% support provincial limits on those charges. Most reject the notion that new homebuyers should bear the cost of growth-related infrastructure.

They are right.

DCs are a hidden tax on homeownership. While municipalities defend them under the principle that "growth should pay for growth," the practical effect is that first-time buyers and young families are forced to shoulder the cost of infrastructure that benefits entire communities. The charges are embedded in housing prices and financed through mortgages.

Reducing DCs won’t solve every housing problem. But it would directly reduce construction costs, improve project viability and lower the final purchase price of homes. It would also send a signal that governments are serious about tackling affordability rather than merely talking about it.

The consequences of failing to act extend far beyond the housing market.

Housing affordability is increasingly shaping life decisions. Young adults are delaying marriage, postponing family formation, and reconsidering where they live. Some are leaving Ontario altogether in search of more affordable opportunities.

Meanwhile, there is growing evidence linking housing costs to falling birth rates. Toronto's fertility rate has fallen to just 1.11 children per woman, lower than Canada's already weak national rate of 1.25, and far below the replacement rate of 2.1. Statistics Canada has found that 37% of Canadians aged 15 to 49 do not believe they can afford to have a child within the next three years.

When housing policy begins influencing whether people can buy homes, stay in a province or have children, the issue is no longer simply about real estate. It’s a question of economic sustainability.

Young Ontarians haven’t given up on homeownership. They still want the stability and security it provides. What they have given up on is the belief that current policies are producing meaningful change.

Until governments permanently reduce the tax burden on housing and DCs, and dramatically increase supply, their skepticism will remain justified. Youth are not losing faith in homeownership. Rather, they are losing faith that governments are prepared to do what it takes to make it attainable again.

Richard Lyall is president of the Residential Construction Council of Ontario (RESCON). He has represented the building industry in Ontario since 1991. Contact him at media@rescon.com.

items.description:
Canada’s banks are bracing themselves for the fallout from the real estate bubble. Last week, the CMHC warned that the share of mortgages in arrears will climb further—especially in Ontario. The banks seem to agree, as the data shows they’ve been preparing for a sharp increase in mortgage losses. The median allowance for mortgage losses […]

The post Canadian Banks Brace For Mortgage Losses, 3x Pre-Pandemic Share appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian banks see more losses from delinquent mortgages in their future—a lot more losses. Mortgage loss expectations have 3x since 2019.
items.body:
Canada’s banks are bracing themselves for the fallout from the real estate bubble. Last week, the CMHC warned that the share of mortgages in arrears will climb further—especially in Ontario. The banks seem to agree, as the data shows they’ve been preparing for a sharp increase in mortgage losses. The median allowance for mortgage losses has more than doubled over the past four years.

Canadian Banks Expect Mortgage Losses To Climb Sharply

Ratio of expected credit losses to total residential mortgage balances.

Source: CMHC; Better Dwelling.

Lenders need to be prepared for losses on bad loans. It doesn’t matter how much borrowers are vetted; the reality is some won’t be fully repaid. To account for this, lenders record an allowance for credit losses—an estimate of the money they do not expect to recover. It reflects expected losses, not just losses that have already occurred. Those expectations have risen sharply.

The CMHC compared each bank’s mortgage portfolio against its allowance for credit losses. The median—half of banks are better, half are worse—had an allowance equivalent to $149 per $100,000 in mortgages in Q2 2026, up 13.2% from a year earlier. That share has climbed 138.1% over the past 4 years, more than doubling. It has roughly tripled (+202.8%) since Q2 2019, back in the before times.

Keep in mind that these measure expected losses relative to mortgage balances. The banks are preparing for higher losses on each dollar lent, and they’ve lent a lot more dollars over that period. Their expectations of losses have grown alongside their mortgage portfolio over the past 7 years.

Canadian Mortgage Losses Expected To Rise Further At Some Banks

The median bank’s increase is sharp, but it hides a much sharper climb at some banks. The 75th percentile, the threshold for the top 25% of banks, saw allowances reach $337 per $100,000 in mortgages, up 47.9% from last year. The share is more than double (+126%) the median, and the highest in the data going back to 2015.

Canadian Mortgage Loss Expectations Grew At 3 In 4 Banks

Most banks expect higher mortgage losses, with roughly 3 in 4 reporting higher allowances than a year earlier. That share was just 53% a year prior, an already tenfold increase from the 5% recorded in Q2 2022. The share of banks reporting higher expected losses has gone from only 1 in 20 banks to 3 in 4 over just four years.

While the amount remains small relative to total mortgage debt, the increase is hard to ignore. Banks are preparing to lose more of each dollar lent, and more lenders expect losses to grow. That also only captures part of the rising pressure, with distress rising even faster among mortgage investment entities (MIEs).

items.title: Ontario Municipalities Begin Slashing Development Charges As Part Of Federal Deal
items.description:
After reaching an $8.8 billion agreement on March 30 to cut development charges, the Governments of Canada and Ontario have been busy finalizing agreements with local governments to implement the changes.

The initiative is officially known as the Development Charge Reduction Program (DCRP) and applications opened on June 1, as previously reported by STOREYS.

The program “will deliver federal and provincial funding over 10 years for housing-enabling infrastructure projects, with funding prioritized for municipalities that reduce development charges for all residential types by 30 per cent to 50 per cent or greater and maintain the reductions for at least three years.”

Municipalities levy development charges on new construction to fund infrastructure, and this program will see the federal and provincial government fund that infrastructure, allowing municipalities to lower the levies.

The first announcements were made in late-August, with Hamilton receiving $572 million and Vaughan receiving $697.2 million.

Hamilton has committed to eliminating development charges on all residential developments from March 30, 2026 to March 31, 2029, reducing the cost of building new homes by up to $100,442 per home.

The $572 million in funding — with the federal government cost-matching the provincial government — will go toward projects like the widening of Barton Street into a five-lane multi-modal road from Fruitland Road to Fifty Road, widening Rymal Road, widening Garner Road, expanding the Woodward water and wastewater treatment plant, and upgrading the capacity of the Greenhill Water Pumping Station.

A few more announcements were made in September, but the pace of announcements hit another gear this month, with agreements with 11 municipalities announced. To date, agreements announced include:

  1. Hamilton: $572 million
  2. Vaughan: $697.2 million
  3. Bradford West Gwillimbury: $94.8 million
  4. Mississauga: $404.1 million
  5. Barrie: $129.2 million
  6. St. Thomas: $19.6 million
  7. Orillia: $11.3 million
  8. Guelph: $48.3 million
  9. Sudbury: $45.3 million
  10. Essex County: $51.2 million
  11. LaSalle: $25.4 million
  12. Essex Town: $8.8 million
  13. Lakeshore: $11.8 million
  14. Kingsville: $8.4 million
  15. Windsor: $77.6 million
  16. Tecumseh: $6.8 million.

In total, the announcements amount to $2.2 billion in infrastructure funding. In most cases, the agreements will see the local government reduce development charges by 30% to 100% from March 30, 2026 to March 31, 2029.

One announcement that was slightly different was that for Mississauga, whose agreement runs from January 29, 2025 to March 31, 2029, reflecting the fact that Mississauga had previously implemented a development charge incentive program on its own, prior to the Canada-Ontario agreement.

Another announcement that was a bit more unique was that for the County of Essex, whose agreement runs from March 30, 2026 to December 31, 2030. According to the announcement, Essex County is reducing development charges on a staggered timeline. The reduction will be 100% for 2026 and 2027, 75% for 2028, 50% in 2029, and 25% in 2030.

The range of infrastructure projects the $2.2 billion in funding will go towards include road, bus, water, and wastewater infrastructure projects that are described as “housing-enabling.”

Ontario is also home to municipalities that do not levy development charges, however, and the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario agreement recognizes that as well. In mid-August, the two governments announced a Non-Development Charge Municipalities Stream (Non-DC Stream) that will allow those governments to also receive infrastructure funding that will enable new housing development.

“Municipalities that do not levy development charges often face challenges funding infrastructure projects because they do not have access to this revenue tool,” said the two governments in the announcement. “At the same time, these municipalities face high construction costs, aging assets and significant infrastructure backlogs.”

The Development Cost Reduction Program began accepting applications under the Non-DC Stream on October 29, 2026, with additional intakes expected to be announced at a later date.

The Development Cost Reduction Program is, of course, just one half of the Canada-Ontario deal, with the other being the 13% HST rebate from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027. The HST relief has sparked market activity in certain areas and segments of the market, although the market has still been fairly subdued.

The HST has also been the envy of the real estate industry in British Columbia, which has continued to push for similar relief. The Governments of Canada and British Columbia reached a deal in June that was similar to the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario deal, but it did not include the tax relief component. The deal did include development charge relief, but the program and agreements were not finalized prior to the snap election held earlier this month.

items.title: B.C. investors turn to retail plazas amid tight supply: report
items.description: Metro Vancouver retail vacancy falls below 1% in some areas: Re/Max
items._ogDesc: Metro Vancouver retail vacancy falls below 1% in some areas: Re/Max
items.body:
Neighbourhood retail vacancy has fallen below one per cent in some Metro Vancouver suburbs as investors turn to established properties, according to a new report.

The Re/Max Canada Fall 2026 Commercial Real Estate Report, released Thursday, found that retail vacancy had fallen below three per cent in downtown Vancouver and less than one per cent in some suburban neighbourhoods.

Conditions across B.C. remain uneven as some other markets, including Kelowna, has been more subdued with limited new building supply weighing on rental conditions and higher costs slowing development, the report said.

“Supply has become increasingly constrained in some of the country’s key commercial markets,” said Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada.

Commercial real estate investors in B.C. are favouring neighbourhood retail plazas and existing industrial properties, as demand for well-located space remains strong. Meanwhile, high construction and financing costs are weighing on new development, according to the report.

“We've seen considerable investment in established, income-producing properties this year, particularly in markets where demand remains strong,” said Kristie Kimnach, executive director of Re/Max Commercial, in a statement.

“The challenge in some of these markets seems to have been finding enough quality products to meet investor demand.”

Neighbourhood shopping plazas and grocery-anchored centres have attracted tenants in sectors including medical services, health, wellness, beauty and food services, the report said.

However, strong demand for industrial space has not necessarily translated into higher sale prices in Greater Vancouver. Industrial sale prices softened even as availability tightened, according to the report.

Kottick said the imbalance between strong demand for established retail space—particularly smaller units in high-demand markets—and a lack of new developments could persist amid higher bond yields and economic uncertainty.

Nationally, 11 of the 12 markets examined reported improving industrial market conditions, measured by increasing absorption and decreasing availability. Retail conditions improved in 10 markets, while multi-family improved in seven markets.

Looking ahead to 2027, Re/Max anticipates a gradual and uneven recovery in Canada's commercial real estate market.

“While demand for established, income-producing properties is expected to remain strong, limited new construction could create further supply challenges in markets where demand continues to grow,” the report said.

The report draws on data and insights from Re/Max brokers and agents across 12 major Canadian markets, comparing activity from January to June 2026 with the same period a year earlier.

items.title: Top Pick at Premier Investment Conference: First Phosphate’s Pure-Play Path to North American LFP Batteries
items.description: John Passalacqua, CEO & Director of First Phosphate Corp., discusses the mineral development and clean tech company's focus on onshoring the lithium iron phosphate battery industry into North America.
items._ogDesc: John Passalacqua, CEO & Director of First Phosphate Corp., discusses the mineral development and clean tech company's focus on onshoring the lithium iron phosphate battery industry into North America.
items.body:
Disseminated on behalf of: First Phosphate Corp.

Clean energy, solar, wind, and energy storage stocks rallied after Democrats won control of both the U.S. House and Senate in the November 3 midterm elections. Those sectors increasingly rely on battery energy storage, where lithium iron phosphate (LFP) is the leading chemistry, and more than 98% of LFP cathode material and battery cells are currently produced in China, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). First Phosphate Corp. (CSE: PHOS | Nasdaq: PHOS | OTCQX: FRSPF | FSE: KD0) is working to onshore that supply chain into North America, starting from a high-purity igneous phosphate mine in Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean, Québec.

In this interview, John Passalacqua, CEO & Director of First Phosphate, discusses the mineral development and clean tech company’s plans to produce phosphoric acid and eventually LFP cathode active material, as demand for a secure domestic battery supply chain grows across energy storage, AI data centres, defence, and electric vehicles.

G7 recognition and export credit support back First Phosphate’s onshoring plan

First Phosphate was represented twice among the 13 critical minerals partnerships and initiatives that Canada announced at the 2026 G7 Summit under the Critical Minerals Resilience and Production Alliance: once for its Bégin-Lamarche mine and once for its planned phosphoric acid plant at Port Saguenay. The company holds definitive offtake agreements for at least 200,000 tonnes of phosphate concentrate and at least 60,000 tonnes of phosphoric acid per year. It has also received letters of intent for support from export credit agencies in Denmark, Switzerland, and Italy. Its feasibility study is expected in the first quarter of 2027.

Pure-play phosphate focus sets First Phosphate apart in LFP battery materials

Unlike many battery materials peers, First Phosphate is focused entirely on phosphate rather than lithium. According to Passalacqua, there are about 150 publicly traded companies worldwide involved in some form of lithium extraction or purification, while phosphate for electrification remains a far less crowded field. “The only company that we know of that is 100% dedicated to [high-purity igneous] phosphate for the lithium iron phosphate battery industry is First Phosphate,” says Passalacqua. He describes phosphate as a 61% slice of the pie of the LFP cathode, compared to a 4% slice for lithium. That gives the company a dedicated position in a segment with few direct competitors.

LFP battery demand drives the market opportunity for igneous phosphate

With LFP chemistry reshaping the battery landscape, First Phosphate is positioned to capture growing demand for a North American LFP battery supply chain. Passalacqua says LFP batteries now make up about 77% of all batteries produced worldwide. They serve a wide range of end markets, including energy storage, AI data centres, defence, marine and agricultural applications, drones, and electric vehicles. The IEA also anticipates a deficit of battery-grade purified phosphoric acid as early as 2030. By focusing on high-purity igneous phosphate from Québec, the company aims to give investors early exposure to a battery materials category that, according to Passalacqua, was not previously available to Nasdaq investors.

Nasdaq listing expands First Phosphate’s access to global investors

First Phosphate recently listed on the Nasdaq Global Market under the ticker PHOS, alongside its existing listing on the Canadian Securities Exchange. Passalacqua notes the company traded more stock over the past four to six weeks after the initial Nasdaq listing than it had in its whole prior history. Many institutional and larger investors require a listing on a major exchange, such as Nasdaq, NYSE, or Euronext, before they can acquire shares. “It really opens up our doors to any investor around the world now,” says Passalacqua. Looking ahead, the company continues to advance its plans for phosphoric acid purification and LFP cathode active materials production.

First Phosphate positioned to build North America’s LFP battery supply chain

As First Phosphate works to onshore the LFP battery industry, it stands at the intersection of electrification and North American supply chain security. Passalacqua attributes the post-midterm rally in clean energy stocks to expectations of stronger policy support for the battery and cleantech sectors. Noting that these technologies all depend on LFP batteries, he expects the theme of onshoring LFP batteries to gain traction in the coming weeks.

With a high-purity igneous phosphate resource and a new Nasdaq listing, the company is positioned to deliver steady progress in Québec’s battery materials sector. That positioning is already drawing attention from institutional investors.

First Phosphate’s pure-play approach to LFP battery materials helped earn it a spot as a Top Pick at Capital Event Management’s (CEM) Muskoka 2026 investment conference, where institutional investors met with a range of public issuers. Top Picks recognize the companies investors most frequently named as standouts from their meetings. Learn more by reading Investor Breakout’s Spotlight on First Phosphate.

Transcript

Transcript lightly edited for clarity, with corrections in bracketed text

John Passalacqua: First Phosphate is a mineral development and clean tech company dedicated to onshoring the lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery industry into North America. We start with a very high-purity igneous phosphate [deposit] in Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean, Québec, and from there, we wish to purify phosphoric acid and eventually produce LFP cathode active materials that go into lithium iron phosphate batteries, which are now about 77% of all batteries produced on planet Earth. [LFP batteries] go into all kinds of different industries, from energy storage to AI data centres, defence, marine, agricultural applications, drones, small bicycles, skateboards, and right up to electric vehicles.

The company had traditionally been listed on the Canadian Securities Exchange. Now we’re listed on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol PHOS. That’s been a great addition for the company. Just over the last four to six weeks [since the Nasdaq listing], we’ve traded more stock than we had in the whole prior history of the company.

So it gets us exposure to the U.S. markets, but it’s also important for the U.S. markets because it’s the first time that the igneous phosphate category has been made available to the U.S. and global investors on Nasdaq. There were a lot of institutional investors and other larger investors that needed us to be listed on a major worldwide exchange such as Nasdaq, NYSE, or Euronext in order to be able to start acquiring shares of the company. Now that we’re listed on that exchange, that meets one of their requirements, as well as some of the others, and they’re able to become involved in the [capital ownership] of the company.

It really opens up our doors to any investor around the world now. If you look at the number of publicly traded companies in the world that are involved in some form of extraction or purification of lithium, there are about 150 of them. Whereas when you look at phosphate, who’s out there in terms of phosphate for electrification? The only company that we know of that is 100% dedicated to [high-purity igneous] phosphate for the lithium iron phosphate battery industry is First Phosphate. We’re one company going after a really big slice of the pie [of the LFP cathode], 61% [for phosphate], whereas when you look at lithium, you’ve got 150 companies going after what is only a 4% slice of the pie [of the LFP cathode].

First Phosphate (CSE: PHOS | Nasdaq: PHOS | OTCQX: FRSPF | FSE: KD0) is a mineral exploration and development and clean technology company dedicated to building and reshoring a vertically integrated mine-to-market supply chain for the LFP battery industry in North America.
